written declarations (article 162 of the ccc)
in writing.– members of the european parliament and united states congress held their 76th inter-parliamentary meeting of the transatlantic legislators’ dialogue in riga on 27 and 28 june. we discussed ways to deepen and strengthen our relationship, and in particular to increase readiness to jointly address the diverse set of global security, economic and environmental challenges that the nations currently face. we exchanged views in three working sessions: 1. achieving growth and jobs through trade. it was highlighted that ttip should be an ambitious, balanced and comprehensive agreement. ambitious approaches on public market access for defined services, mutual recognition of professional qualifications and mobility for professionals and individuals between the nations were discussed. furthermore, the importance of energy issues was upheld in the negotiations. 2. cooperating for energy security. major global challenges to energy security were discussed. the tremendous potential of the united states in this case was highlighted, whilst european energy security was regarded as a solid framework for cooperation amongst member states. 3. reinforcing security and defence cooperation. it was reaffirmed that the key is a strategic partnership. intensifying our cooperation on foreign and security policy in recent times was appreciated.

i have to say, madam president, the lange report uses the phrase 'preventing fiscal dumping'. preventing fiscal dumping aims at tax harmonisation. national tax systems, however, have grown historically and are guided by national tax morals. neither nations nor their tax morals can be harmonized. tax policy is a central part of the national shaping of society and the economy. for reasons of subsidiarity, neither our trading partners nor the eu can dictate national taxes. tax harmonization cannot therefore be part of a free trade agreement. the wording 'autonomy in fiscal policy' is in line with the spirit of the european treaties. i therefore ask you to vote in favour of the amendment 'autonomy in fiscal policy'. thank you, thank you.

member of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a pleasure to be here again in the context of this debate on the market stability reserve. once this parliament ratifies the agreement reached with the council, this reserve will form an integral part of the union's emissions trading scheme, and this scheme is the cornerstone of the european union's climate policy. however, in recent years, the excess of allowances on the market has prevented this scheme from giving the necessary signals to make sufficient low-carbon investments. the stability reserve is designed precisely to tackle this problem and to make the supply of rights more flexible. this is expected to increase market confidence in the emissions trading system and to provide the right price signals in the coming years to achieve our long-term emission reduction targets. in this way, the stability reserve will ensure that we do not miss important opportunities for efficient emission reductions. i would like to thank all the members for their work. i would like to thank in particular the rapporteur, mr belet, and his negotiating team, as well as mr tajani and the alternative rapporteurs from the political groups, for their efforts. the compromise reached provides a solid solution for the major elements of this market stability reserve. let me highlight the most important ones. the commission's original proposal set 2021 as the date for the reserve to become operational. during the debate many mps requested an advance of this date, which has led to the commitment reached for the reserve to be operational in 2019. the undertaking also provides for the transfer of rights withdrawn from the market and rights not allocated to the market stability reserve. and so, the nine hundred million allowances that were withdrawn from the market between 2014 and 2016 will not be returned to the market in 2020 as initially planned. unallocated rights are also transferred to this reserve, which will reduce the risk of regime volatility. the importance of innovation - for me one of the essential elements of this agreement - is also reflected in the compromise text reached. it has been agreed that, in the context of the review of the emissions trading system, consideration should be given to whether 50 million unallocated allowances should be used to accelerate investments in low-carbon technologies. the agreed text also recognises the importance of industrial competitiveness and the risk of carbon leakage for european industry. i can assure you that these two elements will be important issues to be addressed in the context of the proposed revision of the emissions trading system. all the elements i have mentioned will allow a solid architecture of the market stability reserve, as well as ensuring the strengthening of the emissions trading system in the future. we have reached an important milestone with that compromise text, which allows us to focus now on the review of the emissions trading system for the period 2020-2030. last year i committed myself to parliament to translate the elements of the 2030 climate and energy package relating to this emissions trading system into a concrete proposal as soon as agreement is reached on the market stability reserve. i will deliver on this commitment and intend to present a proposal this july on the basis of the consensus reached by the heads of state and government at the european council last october 2014. this proposal will be an important part of the work we are called upon to do to achieve an energy union with a future climate change policy, which is a priority for this commission.
i am speaking on behalf of the ppe group. the commission has already made a number of proposals. i would like to thank mr belet, mr giovanni la via, the chairman of the committee, mr antonio tajani, the rapporteur for the committee on industry, and all the other people who have contributed. the epp will of course vote in favour of the text tomorrow. it was a good proposal put forward by commissioner hedegaard and we have made it even better with the help of her successor, miguel arias cañete. the proposal we have now on the table is more ambitious than what the commission originally proposed. i say this to all those who criticise the proposal because they say it is not enough. we are not only starting two years earlier, but more importantly, contrary to the original proposal, the allowances temporarily taken out in backloading are actually permanently placed in the reserve and the allowances that we have not distributed by 2020 are also placed in the reserve. this is an ambitious climate change initiative to make emissions trading work again. on the other hand - and i fully agree with this - we have made some adjustments which help to avoid the shifting of co2 emissions. we do not want the energy-intensive industry to disappear, but we want it to be up to date with the latest technology through innovation. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we as a parliament have made sure that we have helped industry on this difficult path. i ask industry to accept this outstretched arm, this outstretched hand, and to reject unambitious climate change proposals. i think that is the way forward and the way forward for the commission in its proposal next week, which i am sure will be presented next week: ambitious climate action but with opportunities for industry to continue producing in europe. if we can do that, we will also be a good example for the rest of the world.

acting president of the council. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to begin by expressing my joy, since i am a kind of ghost. i was there ten years ago, during the last luxembourg presidency, and i am very pleased to be back and to be working with you. the motto of the luxembourg presidency is 'creating a union for citizens' and i think our citizens are absolutely entitled to the best possible security. that is why security must be one of our very highest priorities. as you said, mr president, the events that have shocked and shaken us in recent months are precisely what are forcing us to strengthen and, as you have stressed, to adapt even more our means of cooperation to these new challenges of terrorism. for this reason, the luxembourg presidency will focus all its efforts on the implementation and monitoring of the renewed internal security strategy for the european union for the years 2015-2020. if you will allow me, i will recall the main principles of this strategy and tell you what is planned for its implementation. the renewed internal security strategy was adopted by the council on 16 june. it is important to note that this strategy is also based on the elements and principles contained in the commission communication on the european agenda on security of 28 april 2015. it is also important to underline that the renewed strategy should be seen as a common and shared agenda of the european institutions, and both the council and the commission have taken into account the principles set out in your resolution of 17 december 2014. let me now mention a few of the main points. firstly, this strategy identifies three major priorities in the field of internal security of the european union for the coming years. the first is the fight against terrorism - you have just pointed out, we have had the tragic experience of this in recent months - radicalisation leading to terrorism and recruitment and the financing of terrorism and the prevention of these phenomena. for this priority, particular attention will be given to the issue of foreign terrorist fighters, to the reinforcement of external border controls in a systematic and coordinated manner, through relevant databases and on the basis of risk assessments and risk indicators, and by integrating the internal and external aspects of counter-terrorism. the second priority is to prevent and combat large-scale organised crime. the third is to prevent and combat cybercrime and to strengthen cybersecurity. the second element i would like to stress is respect for fundamental rights, the need to respect and defend the rights, freedoms and principles enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union in all actions to create and maintain an area of freedom, security and justice, which is a fundamental principle. a third important element is the need for a comprehensive, multidisciplinary, integrated and information-based approach. access to, availability of and exchange of information in the context of preventing and combating serious transnational organised crime and terrorism will remain crucial issues for the coming years. we must pay particular attention to the interoperability of existing systems. the coordination of investigations and prosecutions in the member states should be encouraged and improved, including for financial investigations aimed at confiscating criminal assets, as well as the effective use of joint investigation teams and mutual legal assistance and mutual recognition procedures. finally, agencies in the field of justice and home affairs, such as europol, eurojust, frontex and ecpol, play an important role in the internal security of the european union. it is necessary to continue to build and support these agencies, which serve the member states. it is worth recalling that our presidency will continue to negotiate with the european parliament on the new europol regulation with the aim of achieving a legislative base enabling the agency to use its full potential in the service of the member states. as regards the other elements to be taken into account, we must first strengthen our operational cooperation and improve our border management capabilities, including the use of the most modern technologies. secondly, we must strengthen the prevention of crime by paying particular attention to organised financial crime, the confiscation of criminal assets and the prevention of terrorist attacks, in particular by preventing radicalisation. secondly, we need to adopt a swift and flexible intelligence-based approach that enables the european union to respond in a comprehensive and coordinated way to emerging and constantly evolving threats. finally, we must consolidate the existing legislative instruments and ensure that they are better applied. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, these are some of the key principles of the renewed strategy. now let us talk about the implementation of this strategy, which we are working very hard to prepare a precise and dynamic work programme. discussions will begin in the council, in particular on the standing committee on operational cooperation on internal security, which is responsible for ensuring proper implementation and regular monitoring of the strategy. this will be done in close cooperation with the commission and involving, where appropriate, other key actors, such as european agencies, for example the european external action service. the presidency intends to discuss in detail for the first time our approach to the implementation of this strategy on 22 and 23 july when cosi and the coordination committee on police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters meet informally in luxembourg. in addition to the methodology for implementation, we intend to start work immediately and to mobilise all our working groups in the council to this end. we will of course take parliament's new resolution into account, as we have done in the past. meps were invited to the conference organised by the italian presidency in september 2014. the chairman of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs was a key speaker at the event. the presidency, the commission and the member states used the conclusions of this conference to draw up the council conclusions on the renewed strategy. we also used the commission's final report on the implementation of the internal security strategy, which took up the european parliament's resolution on this subject. i therefore remain confident in our ability to develop a common approach to the implementation of the strategy. the chairman of cosi will inform the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs of this work. in conclusion, ladies and gentlemen, we look forward to your new resolution. i am convinced that many of your recommendations are already reflected in the renewed strategy and that we will take them into account when implementing the strategy. i am thinking, for example, of the best use of existing instruments before creating new ones, the need to adopt a comprehensive and balanced approach taking into account the principle of proportionality, and then the need for more effective and more operational cooperation between the member states, the attention to be paid to the judicial dimension and the role of the european parliament and national parliaments in ensuring democratic control of the implementation of the strategy. i thank you for your attention and i look forward to listening carefully to your debate.
member of the commission.– madam president, thank you for the opportunity offered by your oral question to debate further with you on the european agenda on security. i also want to express my thanks to claude moraes for his support. thank you also for the draft resolution, which is to be voted on two days from now, and which i will of course take into consideration. i hope that the resolution will have the wide support of this house. as i – and many among you as well – have said several times, we need to show our citizens that we all work together on the basis of a shared agenda. today’s debate happens, as was mentioned before by claude, on the 10th anniversary of the 7 july terrorist attacks in london. sadly, it also happens only a few days after another series of unacceptable terrorist attacks. even if these are addressed specifically tomorrow, as you know, it shows that our security has to remain high on our agenda. one year ago, in june 2014, the european council asked the union to renew and update the previous internal security agenda 2010-2014. all the institutions have provided their contribution to this process in a coordinated fashion. following the last commission’s report on the implementation of the internal security strategy (iss), both the council and parliament paved the way in december 2014 for the commission to develop its european agenda on security adopted on 28 april 2015. last month, the council adopted, on the basis of the commission’s agenda, conclusions on the development of the renewed european union internal security strategy 2015-2020. the renewed internal security strategy is the result of this process, and it constitutes a major achievement for the european union. it was endorsed at the highest level by the european council at its june summit, both in terms of content and in terms of cooperation among the institutions. in terms of content, the new strategy sets out the shared vision of the three institutions for the next five years on what needs to be done at union level to make europe more secure for the sake of its citizens, societies and economies. it identifies the main priorities for the union’s actions, namely tackling terrorism and radicalisation, disrupting organised crime and fighting against cybercrime. from the institutional point of view, the commission, parliament and the council have acted together, with each one offering their strategic contribution to the security strategy in line with the spirit of the lisbon treaty. as the commission put it in its european agenda on security: successful implementation on renewed internal security strategy depends on the political commitment of all actors concerned to do more, and of course to do better. this includes not only eu institutions, but also member states and eu agencies. in addition to active engagement, coordinated and coherent action is a prerequisite. i therefore welcome the european parliament’s call to the commission and the council to work together towards effective implementation and to engage in an interinstitutional dialogue. the commission is fully committed to maintaining a constant dialogue with the european parliament on internal security matters. the commission undertakes to update the european parliament and the council twice a year on the implementation of the agenda. this will be the opportunity to take stock, together, of both the achievements and the challenges faced, and to exchange views on the state of eu internal security. in addition, transparency contributes to increasing citizens’ confidence in security policies. the commission will therefore set up an eu security consultative forum to further enhance transparency and participation. this forum will bring together member states, the european parliament, eu agencies and representatives of civil society, academia and the private sector. the format of the forum will be finalised in due course, and the european parliament will be kept informed. in the same context, the commission will also develop performance indicators for key eu institutions. now, when speaking about implementation of the agenda, an important aspect is resources, including those of the eu agencies. the european agenda on security has set, as one of its key principles, the need to ensure better application and full implementation of existing instruments. pursuant to this principle, implementing the agenda will centre on consolidating the existing instruments and reprioritising available resources. the principle also applies to the agencies: for instance, the european counter-terrorism centre within europol is also included. it is meant to bring together anti-terrorism law enforcement capabilities, thereby pooling resources and maximising the use of the existing legal structures, services and tools already available. of course, ensuring sufficient resources to eu agencies is crucial for them to be able to perform their work and to fully contribute to the goals of the agenda. as envisaged by the european agenda on security, the commission will launch a reflection on how to maximise the contribution of all jha agencies through closer inter-agency cooperation. the commission invites the member states to assign appropriate resources at the national level and to reinforce their efforts in seconding their national experts to agencies. in a situation of limited budgets, all efforts must be made to prioritise and reallocate. increasing the agencies’ budget is the only other way to increase resources. as you know, the commission is following the interinstitutional agreement of december 2013 that foresees that all eu institutions and bodies – as well as all agencies – reduce their total staffing levels by 5% over five years. this does not prejudge the budgetary rights of the european parliament and the council, but any increase in the agencies’ resources would require the firm commitment and agreement of both branches of the budgetary authority.

a new global partnership to meet the inseparable challenge of poverty eradication and sustainable development. this partnership will guide the international community for years to come. the european union and its member states should not miss this historic event. this partnership must be based on the principles of universality and shared and mutual responsibilities. we will have to take into account the capacities of each individual and involve a wide range of stakeholders. this new global partnership will also have to promote human rights, equality, non-discrimination, democratic institutions, good governance and the rule of law. it should enable everyone to participate actively and ensure environmental sustainability and respect for the limits of our planet. women's rights, gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls, which are already an end in themselves, are essential means of implementation and will have to be promoted at all levels. i am thinking overall vision adapted to the change in the world order. the addis ababa conference which opens next monday should not be limited to assessing the progress made in implementing the monterrey consensus and the doha declaration. it must be forward-looking, allow for an integrated approach to all means of implementation and focus on the mobilisation and efficient use of all financial and other resources. the european union and its member states must continue to uphold this fundamental principle, which has been the cornerstone of the monterrey process. national public funds are the largest source of stable and directly available funding for most governments and are therefore at the heart of sustainable development financing. national governments have the primary responsibility for mobilising and making the best use of these public resources. the conference should result in an integrated approach to the implementation and financing of the new partnership. it is a question of december. while financial resources remain important, even essential - national public funds, private funds, innovative financing, international aid - we must also put non-financial means of post-2015 programme. it will need to encompass national, regional and global levels and involve all governmental and non-governmental actors in its implementation. ladies and gentlemen, the european adopted a position on official development assistance, which reaffirms the collective commitment of the union and the member states to reach the target of 0.7% of gross national income devoted to official development assistance by the deadline set by the post-2015 programme, as well as their priority commitment to the least developed countries. it should facilitate the active participation of the european union and its member states in the ongoing international negotiations and contribute to their success. the success of this global partnership depends on the contribution of all of us. we post-2015 agenda that brings the transformation and inclusion we need.

president of the european council.– mr president, i would first like to wish the luxembourg presidency all the best. there is a very challenging six months ahead and i look forward to the closest under the greatest migratory pressure. we agreed on the relocation and resettlement of 60 000 refugees over the next two years. for clarity, the scheme will complement existing national efforts, with eu countries now receiving 600 000 asylum applications per year. yes, the discussion was difficult and at times divisive. to my mind, it was the first time european leaders have had such an honest exchange on the refugee question. the european council chose to keep to the voluntary approach agreed at the special european council in april. there is a balance to be struck between national sovereignty and action at european level in this matter. now we have an agreement with which we can work, and on which we can build. the luxembourg presidency is receiving voluntary pledges from member states on both relocation and resettlement. based on progress so far, we hope that the numbers agreed at the european council will be reached. in the light of the ongoing emergency, leaders new european union strategy on foreign and security policy for june next year. we also agreed to use eu funding to support collective efforts to invest in the future of european defence. finally, we discussed economic matters, most notably the report on completing economic and monetary union (emu), published on 22 june. the report makes clear that the priority in building a deeper monetary union president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, friday 26 june, a kind of black day, was marked by several terrorist attacks. this time, three countries were hit almost simultaneously: france, kuwait and tunisia. these attacks have once again reminded us of the despicable nature of terrorism and especially of those who sponsor and carry it out. our response must be firm and united. on 26 june, the european council made it clear that we must step up our action against these terrorist threats. the fight against terrorism is one of the most important challenges and a top priority for our open and democratic societies. our presidency will make this a top priority. we will build on the work undertaken by our predecessors, taking into account both internal and external aspects of security. the luxembourg presidency will work to ensure that the european union adopts a coherent approach to the fight against terrorism, covering both the internal and external aspects of security, namely a strong and fruitful cooperation between the member states, the commission, the european external action service and the european union coordinator. we have instruments such as europol, eurojust, frontex and ecpol. these instruments must be given the necessary means and resources. in response to the attacks in paris in january, the heads of state or government adopted a declaration on 12 february based on three pillars: ensuring the safety of citizens, preventing radicalisation, protecting values and, finally, cooperating with international partners. the union counter-terrorism coordinator has submitted to the council and the european council a comprehensive report on the implementation of these measures. on 28 april the commission adopted the european programme on security. we discussed it yesterday. the fight against terrorism is one of the main priorities, the strong international dimension of terrorism has been underlined and our action must be on the same international level. on 9 february, the foreign affairs council adopted conclusions on the fight against terrorism, aimed specifically at strengthening cooperation with the countries of north africa, the middle east and the gulf, as well as with turkey and the balkan countries. a number of capacity building projects in the field of counter-terrorism were approved. workshops on this topic have already been held in lebanon and turkey. the eu counter-terrorism coordinator led an inter-service mission to tunisia, following which the high representative proposed a series of support measures to the tunisian prime minister. finally, a strategic communication task force was set up to develop an awareness and communication strategy for the arab world. we must also actively pursue our cooperation with the united nations, nato, the council of europe and other international organisations, as well as our bilateral cooperation with our main partners, such as the united states. on 16 june, the ministers of the interior concluded that tangible progress had been made in recent months. it is essential to prevent radicalisation in our own countries and in our partner countries. how is it possible that young people in our countries, who have been to our schools, are attracted to these terrorist networks that preach unheard-of violence? there is a lot of work to be done on this, and it has to be done on many levels: education, integration, our values. to this end, the centre of excellence, called the european radicalisation awareness network, is about to be launched. other measures should be taken, such as the reinforcement of the application of the schengen framework: documents and persons should be subject to more systematic checks in the relevant databases through a risk-based approach. this approach was finalised on 15 june and will now be implemented. the schengen practical manual for border guards has been updated. a unit for reporting internet content was set up within europol on 1 july to speed up the pooling of resources and to intensify cooperation with the sector. the aim is to reduce the scale and impact of terrorist propaganda and violent and extremist propaganda on the internet, while fully respecting, of course, fundamental rights. the council expects to be able to adopt a decision on the signing, on behalf of the european union, of the additional protocol to the council of europe convention on the prevention of terrorism, which would make it an offence to travel by foreign terrorist fighters. externally, and in close partnership with countries where the terrorist threat is particularly present, we must help these countries to combat also the social causes of terrorism, such as the frustrating unemployment of young people, which thus becomes a favourable terrain for recruiting new terrorists. tunisia is, unfortunately, an example of this. the luxembourg presidency will be actively involved in this. we will be proposing next week a new cooperation initiative with the maghreb countries on youth employment and vocational training, because i believe that we must tackle at the root the problem of young people tempted by the terrorist adventure, whether in syria or in their own country. i would now like to return to the question of radicalisation. the speed with which this phenomenon is spreading is a cause for concern. in some cases, young people become radicalised in a very short period of time, as little as two months. we will be holding a conference on 19 and 20 october on the subject of rehabilitation and radicalisation in prisons, which often reveal these young terrorists who are ready to act. the treatment of foreign fighters returning to our societies is another issue that we will have to address. commissioner jourová also reoriented funding to include the fight against terrorism in the funding programmes launched this year under the justice sector. we need to strengthen the means to counter the use of the internet and social networks by terrorists to spread their hateful propaganda and to radicalise and recruit young people. we must spread messages to counter terrorist propaganda and launch concerted and well-organised campaigns, including through the media. more needs to be done, in particular, on the decommissioning of firearms and the strengthening of the fight against arms trafficking. we must also redouble our efforts in the field of information exchange. the informal meeting of the ministers of justice and the ministers of the interior in luxembourg tomorrow will include discussions on improving the exchange of information between the intelligence services and the police. as i said yesterday, the implementation of the renewed internal security strategy for the union for 2015-2020 is a priority for the luxembourg presidency and can be a very active and useful instrument in the fight against terrorism. we must act decisively, and above all we must attack the root causes of this scourge, but we must not fall into the trap of those who are waging this terrorist war against our peoples and our states, namely, to weaken our democratic systems and our values. democracies are all the stronger if their action also ensures respect for human rights, which must remain our guiding principle.
member of the commission.– mr president, the appalling attacks perpetrated on friday, 26 june 2015, in france, tunisia, kuwait and somalia demonstrate once again the brutality and inhumanity of terrorists. let me first extend, on behalf of the commission, our condolences to the families of the victims and express our moral support and our sympathy to the countries affected in europe and beyond. i wish to condemn these acts of terror in the strongest terms and reaffirm our determination to address collectively this threat. we need to provide security to our citizens while upholding our values. of course, we face constantly-evolving threats, and the numerous victims of this year’s attacks remind us of this reality. investigations are still being carried out by the competent national authorities. the available information tends to demonstrate that the atrocities committed in saint-quentin-fallavier, in sousse and in kuwait bear the hallmarks of daesh’s despicable ideology of intolerance. their objective is to instil terror. it is also relevant to note that terrorists are focusing on soft targets, such as religious buildings or tourist resorts. this commission, as you know, has been working closely with the member states to identify areas in which the european union can make a real difference in fighting terrorism and radicalisation. we have been working closely with member states to enhance our capacity to address this threat. in april the commission presented the european agenda on security. the agenda places terrorism very high among the future priorities. it embodies a concept of security that encompasses the rule of law and fundamental rights. the agenda sets out a number of actions to counter the threat posed by terrorism. we have started working vigorously on their implementation. let me now focus on some of the ongoing work of high political and practical significance. first, preventing radicalisation remains essential. the radicalisation awareness network centre of excellence, to be launched in september, will take the work of the existing ran further. i consider the work of ran and the whole prevention element of the counter-terrorism policy at eu level to be crucial. secondly, on 1 july 2015, the internet referral unit was established at europol. it will be fully operational within 12 months. the mission of the internet referral unit is to identify terrorist material in different languages and to help secure swift removal. third, by the end of the year, the commission will formally launch an eu-level forum together with the internet industry. this will allow us to discuss how we can reduce the accessibility of online terrorist material and counter terrorist propaganda on the internet and in social media. a first workshop under the forum will be held on 24 july 2015, with experts from the industry and the law enforcement communities. fourthly, the protection of external borders is crucial. with a view to supporting member states in performing enhanced and targeted border checks, the commission finalised – in close cooperation with member states – a first set of common risk indicators. europol and frontex are assisting member states in their implementation, and we have just revised their handbook for border guards. in the framework of the european union’s customs risk management strategy, work is going on to enhance cooperation and information exchange between customs and law enforcement and to detect suspicious movements of goods. fifthly, in order to trace and disrupt terrorist financing, we are working on the strengthening of cooperation between financial intelligence units. let me also stress that the recently-adopted anti-money laundering directive improves the tools to address terrorist financing. sixthly, as stated in the european agenda on security, we also need to better protect our citizens and critical infrastructures from terrorist threats. this work includes practical tools such as the guidance material that my services have recently developed on soft target protection. we are also upgrading the european programme for critical infrastructure protection, which will help to prevent attacks and failures and to improve preparedness and the response to incidents. seventhly, as civil aviation remains the preferred target of terrorists, the commission continues to work to increase aviation security and safety. a joint process is being developed with member states to assess the risks from conflict zones and support the issuing of recommendations to airlines and the public. eighthly, let me mention now eu-pnr, which is an important component of our security agenda. i wish to express my thanks to parliament for your efforts in bringing to completion the eu legislation on pnr. i am confident that we can all continue to work together in such a constructive way so that the co-legislators can agree on a text that adheres to the highest standards of data protection and that is, at the same time, effective. ninthly, the recent attacks illustrate the need for better international coordination and cooperation. the attack in tunisia was extremely brutal and symbolic, as it targeted tourism – a vital economic sector for the country. it was an attack on tunisia’s hospitality and its long-standing and friendly relations with europe. we must stand by our tunisian partners and show solidarity. increasing their security will also contribute to enhancing our security. in the wake of the bardo museum attack, i travelled to tunis and discussed, with my counterparts, how the european union can provide support. we need to work together in tackling the root causes of radicalisation, detecting terrorists’ travel and building security capabilities and capacities. honourable members, we have worked a lot in the past six months and we have made good progress in a number of areas, but the recent attacks remind us that a lot still needs to be done. we owe this to the victims, and we owe it to our citizens and our partners. let us therefore continue, with resolve and determination, in our joint efforts against terrorism and radicalisation.

rapporteur.– madam president, there are two ways to look at this copyright evaluation report. on the one hand, it is a great step forward. it recognises that users of copyrighted works have rights – a foreign concept to the current copyright directive. according to the directive, rights holders have rights and users have exceptions to those rights. these exceptions are optional to the member states. they can simply be disabled by a contract or by technological restrictions. circumventing those restrictions is illegal, even for legitimate purposes. so it is illegal to make a book that has a technological lock available to a blind person, but the terms of service that simply erase an exception to copyright are completely legal. the copyright directive, so far, protects digital locks more than it protects the people. this report calls for a clear set of european consumers’ rights. it states that copyright exceptions must not be overridden by a contract, and that you cannot charge a levy for private copying on the one hand, but then, on the other hand, use technology that makes private copying impossible. this report calls for interoperability and cross-border access, so you should be able to buy and to use works on any device or in any country. it sides with the right to education and with allowing libraries, museums and archives to do their jobs in the digital world and to make our shared cultural heritage accessible to anybody, regardless of their social status. but, at the same time, this report is also a tragically-missed opportunity. just a year ago, thousands of europeans participated in a public consultation on copyright, and they expressed how they come into daily conflict with a law that is unfit for the digital age. then commissioner kroes recognised that copyright must be radically reformed so that it would not become irrelevant. president juncker announced his goal to tear down national silos in copyright, and commissioner ansip boldly took on geo-blocking. the message was clear: now is the time to act decisively. not from this parliament. parliament recognises, in the report, that 28 different copyright laws are too complicated, but still it considers our cultures to be so different that we cannot possibly agree on simple things like the fact that drawing a caricature should not require permission, a rights holder should not forbid a journalist from quoting a work in order to criticise it, or public pictures of public space should remain royalty—free. this parliament is at its best when it is the voice of the people. it has rejected the acta treaty because the people we represent embrace the internet as an integral part of their reality. with copyright, you have seen tens of thousands of your young people on the streets opposing acta and holding signs saying ‘this video is not available in your country’. you have had thousands of responses to the consultation on copyright asking for more europe in copyright law. you have had half a million petitioners demanding freedom of panorama. now you have the chance to take up this call and to update copyright law to the digital age. personally, i wonder if this report, as it stands, is really the best that we can do if this is what european leadership looks like. i also hope that you, my colleagues, will wonder why people considered it necessary to form a party that is solely based on reforming copyright, to give it the ridiculous name of the pirate party and to elect me here to the european parliament to tell you that copyright reform is urgently needed. i am hoping that, when the reform from the commission comes, my colleagues will be bolder in demanding european copyright and common rules for everybody. i also hope that we can make sure that parliament is not just following the commission proposal but is also a decisive player in making sure that copyright is fit for the digital age and understandable to ordinary people.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. in an open society, prohibitions should be the exception. copyright law follows an opposite logic. the phrase "all rights reserved" actually means: everything is forbidden that is not exceptionally allowed. the use of photographs, videos and images permanently displayed in public places should continue to be possible without restrictions. the copyright extremism has to be stopped. the freedom of panorama must be guaranteed. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union's cultural heritage.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. the report could be entitled: free access and fair remuneration. the report has succeeded in striking a balance between the interests of cultural professionals in fair remuneration and the free access of internet users to online services. in the digital age, artists must be able to make a living from their work, and we do not want to see any form of criminalisation of internet users. other important findings of the report are: the rights of cultural creators are strengthened in relation to other rights holders. the commission is proposing to set up a european network of national authorities responsible for the protection of copyright and related rights. exceptions are made for educational purposes and also for libraries. the issue of freedom of panorama has recently been discussed in the public sphere. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. these widespread reports are now dissolving into complacency. the european parliament must send a clear message today: freedom of panorama is not being compromised. we should therefore vote against the corresponding paragraph 46. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the european copyright directive was adopted in 2001. we need to modernise copyright law to meet the requirements of the cross-border digital single market. i think it is important to strike a fair and reasonable balance between the interests of users and rights holders. that's what copyright is all about. copyright must not only be seen from the perspective of the consumer, but also from the perspective of the creative work. i therefore ask you again today, ladies and gentlemen, to support amendment no 1. it does not require - i would like to emphasize this again - that a european right to protection of performance be introduced. the commission has not yet received the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. let me read the amendment again. it invites the commission to 'examine how quality journalism can be maintained in the digital age and to come forward with a proposal to ensure media diversity, in particular taking into account the important role played by journalists, authors and media service providers such as press publishers'. for me, media diversity is not just about everyone being able to express their opinions and communicate. i appreciate the work of the journalists, the editors, the writers, even those who do the research, who sort for their readers, who categorize, who comment. that's what i call quality journalism. that is why, ladies and gentlemen, i have tabled this amendment and i would be very pleased if you could support it in the vote this afternoon. in writing. ‒ the commission's objective of promoting transparency and greater involvement of shareholders is generally welcomed. the text now adopted by the plenary represents a considerable improvement on the report adopted by the committee. the main positive aspects are the freedom of action granted to the member states, for example in the regulatory framework for remuneration policy or in transactions with related companies, and the more flexible exercise of control by shareholders, which is considered more feasible than a rigid focus on the annual general meeting. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be required to provide information on the use of the euro in their national currency. the call for greater involvement of employees and civil society in corporate governance, and for these to be aligned with undefined environmental and social policy objectives, also dilutes the shareholder-oriented draft law. i was therefore unable to agree to the draft report. i abstained from the vote.
in writing. ‒ the cdu/csu group in the epp group voted against country-by-country reporting in today's vote on the sergio cofferati report. we are not opposed to country-specific reporting in principle. for example, we welcome the provisions in the accounting directive (2013/34/eu), which is to be evaluated by the eu commission by 2018, and the directive on the taking up and pursuit of the business of credit institutions and the prudential supervision of credit institutions and investment firms (crd iv, 2013/36/eu). however, before these provisions are extended to other sectors, we call for a thorough impact assessment by the eu commission. in addition, developments in country-by-country reporting in the oecd action plan against the cutting of profits and shifting of profits of multinational enterprises (beps) need to be taken into account in order to ensure a level playing field. in addition, it is essential that smes and medium-sized enterprises are exempted from additional reporting burdens.

in writing. ‒ yesterday we voted on the market stability reserve for the eu's greenhouse gas emissions trading system. the european commission has proposed to reform the eu emissions trading system (eu ets) by introducing a market stability reserve (msr) from 2021. the msr allows the commission to issue or refuse additional co2 allowances in order to protect the eu ets from cyclical fluctuations and to cancel the excess supply of allowances that has accumulated in recent years. however, european industries have sounded the alarm, pointing to the competitiveness, deindustrialisation of europe and the impact of the ukrainian crisis, which is turning attention to the security of energy supply. however, in october 2014, eu leaders reached an agreement on the 2030 climate and energy package. they expressly support the commission's proposal on msr and that additional co2 allowances be issued beyond 2020 for the industrial sectors that are particularly affected by the shift of co2 emissions. the report includes the following compromises: (i) entry into force in 2019; (ii) co2 emissions shifting: the commission is to draw up a proposal; (iii) innovation fund: an additional fund to support breakthrough technologies is to be set up. that is why i voted for it.

the next item is the debate on the report by cristian-silviu buşoi, on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending regulation (ec) no 1007/2009 on trade in seal products (com (2015) 0045 - c8-0037/2015 - 2015/0028 (cod)) (a8-0186/2015).
member of the commission.– madam president, first and foremost, let me thank and congratulate the rapporteur, mr buşoi, and his colleagues for their commitment and thorough and also speedy work on the commission proposal to amend the basic regulation on trade in seal products. the amendment had become necessary after the wto ruling in june last year. while the ruling upheld the eu ban on marketing of seal products, the wto concluded that the exceptions provided by the eu for inuit and other indigenous communities and for maritime resource management had some discriminatory effects. we believe that the constructive cooperation between the institutions has led to a very good result. it will enable the eu to comply with its international obligations under the wto by the very challenging deadline which we were given for implementation and which will expire next month (on 18 october, to be precise). this is a very important step for the credibility of the eu, as one of the main users of the wto dispute settlement mechanism, in implementing its wto obligations. we are very pleased to have come to the end of this process of amending our seal regime and making it compliant with wto rules. it is a politically sensitive issue for many involved, and we are satisfied that a balanced compromise has been reached. throughout the process, the commission has engaged with all the relevant stakeholders and also those member states particularly concerned with the proposal. we believe that this dialogue has been very constructive and that its results are reflected in the outcome of this process. the final result upholds the ban with a meaningful indigenous-communities exception and addresses all the shortcomings identified by the wto, such as the need for removal of the marine resource management exception. it provides for a balanced approach between fulfilling the eu’s international trade obligations and addressing the legitimate concerns of inuit communities and member states affected by the changes. furthermore, some specific requests by the european parliament were taken on board in the compromise text, such as the provisions requiring the commission to regularly evaluate the regulation, as well as to inform the public about the ban and its exception. the commission has made it clear that we fully support the outcome as far as the substance is concerned. on some procedural issues, changes made to the commission’s proposal in the course of the negotiations require us to make two statements relating to horizontal institutional issues, which we have forwarded to the european parliament services for recording in the minutes. firstly, on the use of the no-opinion clause for the adoption of implementing acts, and, secondly, on the use of the comitology procedure for issuing technical guidance notes. commission’s statements on: 1) the use of the no-opinion clause for the adoption of implementing acts ‘ the commission underlines that it is contrary to the letter and to the spirit of regulation 182/2011 (oj l 55 of 28.2.2011, p. 13) to invoke article 5 § 4, subparagraph 2, point b) in a systematic manner. recourse to this provision must respond to a specific need to depart from the rule of principle which is that the commission may adopt a draft implementing act when no opinion is delivered. given that it is an exception to the general rule established by article 5 § 4 recourse to subparagraph 2, point b), cannot be simply seen as a ‘discretionary power’ of the legislator, but must be interpreted in a restrictive manner and thus must be justified.’2) the use of comitology procedure for issuance of technical guidance notes ‘the commission notes that the co-legislators have included in the final compromise text a provision according to which the non-binding guidance notes under article 3(6) will be adopted by examination procedure. the commission is of the view that the adoption of non-binding guidelines by the commission should not be subject to the control mechanism under regulation 182/2011 since the commission has its own autonomous right under the treaty to issue such guidance. considering the urgent need to meet the wto requirements and deadlines the commission does not oppose the solution favoured by the co-legislators in this particular file. this is without prejudice to the negotiations of the inter-institutional agreement on better law-making, as well as the position the commission will take on similar matters in the future.’
i am speaking on behalf of the ppe group. the commission is not prepared to accept this. i would also like to thank mr cristian buşoi for his work on this draft implementing regulation for the implementation of the wto decision. there can be no doubt that the european union, the european single market, is subjecting its legislation to the requirements of the wto, and i am very grateful to the committee on the internal market and consumer protection for having done so quickly. the question we are faced with, however, is how we can reconcile environmental protection, animal welfare on the one hand, with other economic and political constraints in the future. the exception we have found takes due account of these balance considerations. we must ensure that the legal options that have been allowed in this wto-compliant implementation process are also allowed in the end, so that the legislation has the value that we actually want to give it. in this respect, commissioner, we shall have to see how this legislation actually works in the end, but the european parliament's implementation process has been successful. thank you very much.
i have to say, madam president, in 2009, we enforced a blanket ban on the sale of products for commercialisation, and that was a good thing. we have rightly made an exception for the inuit, because we know very well that this is part of their livelihood. without this hunting and without the products they get from this hunting, they simply cannot survive, and so we cannot simply say, this exception cannot be made, or it is too complicated, or it is too difficult to control. no, we have to respect that these people also need a livelihood, and we said, yes, we have to do that. the second exception was a more difficult one: the conservation of marine resources, what can one understand by that? what can be hidden behind it? i think it's a good thing that we've now removed that exception entirely. we have done a good job and i think we can accept this compromise tomorrow with confidence because it really does put the right emphasis and it has also been taken into account that in the future we will have to look again at how this really affects, especially the inuit, because we do not want to destroy their livelihoods. thank you so much.

mr president, first of all congratulations to rapporteur ferrara and her colleagues for compiling this excellent report on the situation of fundamental rights in the eu. it highlights the discrepancies between freedoms promised in law and the freedoms denied when people put them to the test. anyone whose fundamental rights have been denied deserves our support, whether they are taking to the streets of barcelona in defiance of national gag laws, whether they are rallying across the continent in support of the citizens’ initiative or, indeed, demanding access to documents from ongoing ttip negotiations without 95% of their contents being redacted. the report also takes a decisive stance against fundamental rights violations in the self-proclaimed war on terror, and it does not buy into the myth purported, for example, by the epp shadow that blanket surveillance could guarantee our safety. safeguarding the rights to be informed about government actions, to have one’s privacy respected, to speak out against injustice and to participate in the political process are all fundamental rights vital to democracy. it is this parliament’s duty to safeguard these rights, and i count upon my colleagues to adopt the ferrara report and to ensure that comprehensive monitoring of the member states’ fundamental rights obligations is ensured.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. it is surprising that such a report on the human rights situation in europe should simply omit the fact that there is discrimination through political persecution in the eu countries. the first is in greece, austria and the federal republic of germany. there are bans on opinions, bans on professions, bans on meetings, bans on hotels, bans on houses. in germany, 12 000 investigations are opened against patriotic citizens every year, and over 1 000 are in prison, most notably my friend horst mahler, who was sentenced to 12 and a half years for his opinion alone, and whose leg was amputated only in august because he was not given sufficient opportunity to move in a german prison. mr timmermans, you say that you are impartial. if you leave that out, you are not impartial, because fundamental rights are indivisible.
the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' in the context of the directive. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. the european union sets high standards for each candidate country, and no country can become a member of the eu unless it has a clear commitment to democracy, the rule of law and respect for fundamental rights, and above all if these values are not also upheld. the eu is a community of values, and it should therefore be taken for granted that fundamental rights are fully guaranteed even after a country joins, but unfortunately this is often not the case. why should the eu be able to monitor the respect of european values effectively only before a country joins, but not afterwards? there is an article 7 in the eu treaty, but it is a blunt sword because of the many obstacles to its application. the commission and the council have taken the first steps to remedy this situation. this is all very welcome, but it is not enough! what is needed is a genuine fundamental rights mechanism, with continuous monitoring of the fundamental rights situation in each country and with country-specific reports published regularly. the eu institutions must be able to intervene in good time in the event of serious violations of fundamental rights in a member state. the core issue here is one of credibility. objective criteria and a transparent process would, in my view, ensure that no country is unfairly singled out. i support mrs ferrara's report and i hope that if the report is adopted the council and the commission will also take up the call for the establishment of a fundamental rights mechanism. thank you very much.

the next item on the agenda is the brief presentation of the report by mr richard corbett on the procedures and practices for the hearings of members of the commission lessons to be drawn from the 2014 procedure (2015/2040(ini)) (a8-0197/2015).
first vice-president of the commission.– mr president, i am tempted to ask mr arnott how many candidates he can hear in the house of commons, let alone in the house of lords, but we shall not go into that debate. i want to thank the rapporteur, mr corbett, for his excellent and well—reflected report on a topic that members will understand is of great relevance for the commission. the commission welcomes and fully supports the pursued objective of making the hearings a more flexible and dynamic exchange. the hearings not only allow for parliament’s scrutiny of the commission, in line with the treaty, but also provide an important window for citizens on the workings of the union. incidentally, i was a minister in a national government, then i became a commissioner and all of a sudden, in the media, i went from being in some quarters a politician to an anonymous bureaucrat, whereas the scrutiny i went through in this parliament was much tougher than the scrutiny i had to face in the national parliament in the netherlands before becoming a minister. by the way, in quite a number of member states – because the second objection you always get is ‘unelected’ – how many governments do you suppose there are (i do not know the exact number, but there are quite a number of governments) where ministers are not elected? parliaments are all elected like this parliament. so it is very often simply a matter of perception. for the commission, it is of foremost importance that the hearings are conducted in an open, fair and consistent manner. in particular, hearings for all commissioners-designate should follow the same approach for questions and answers, both in the written and in the oral phase, and for the evaluation of each commissioner-designate. for vice-presidents-designate, who have a horizontal responsibility spanning the competences of a larger number of ep committees, it is indeed appropriate to foresee that hearings are carried out in an adapted format, such as an open conference of presidents. more generally, the confirmation period should be enough time to ensure that the new commission can take up office immediately on the normal expiry of the previous commission’s mandate. in this context, the commission supports the call on member states to make timely and gender-balanced nominations for candidate commissioners. as to the conduct of the hearings, the commission supports the envisaged increase of written questions from five to seven, on condition that sub—questions are abandoned. the commission also welcomes the limitation of questions in the oral phase to 25, with the possibility of immediate follow—up questions. in principle, the commission supports parliament’s objective to ensure that the hearing process is accessible and transparent for eu citizens. hearings are, however, for the elected members of parliament to exercise their scrutiny on commissioners-designate. therefore, it is the right of members of the european parliament to directly put questions to commissioners—designate. the commission is open to considering how best to facilitate parliament’s examination of potential conflicts of interest of commissioners-designate. should the commission consider it appropriate to come forward with an amendment to its code of conduct, it will seek parliament’s opinion, as foreseen by the framework agreement. to ensure that commissioners-designate are evaluated exclusively with regard to their personal competencies and knowledge of the envisaged portfolio, the commission maintains that the results of the evaluation of each commissioner-designate should be published individually within 24 hours after completion of her/his evaluation. as for horizontal issues affecting the composition and structure of the commission as a whole, the commission recalls the need to fully respect each institution’s competences and prerogatives. the commission looks forward to examining the concrete proposals for amendments to parliament’s rules of procedure regarding the hearings of commissioners—designate. i would like once again to thank mr corbett for a job very well done from the commission’s perspective.

the next item is the brief presentation of the report by ms marietje schaake on 'human rights and technology: the impact of spying and surveillance systems on human rights in third countries' (2014/2232(ini)) (a8-0178/2015).
the rapporteur. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. first of all, i would like to thank all my colleagues - not only in my own group but also in the other groups - for their support in the preparation of the report on family businesses in europe. it was a really nice and very interest-oriented collaboration. you probably all know the famous names of companies like de longhi, lego, heineken, oetker, clarins and whatnot producers of high quality products, known not only in their home countries but also beyond the borders of europe. all these companies have one thing in common, ladies and gentlemen: these are family businesses that have been around for decades and are doing well. but it is not just the large, successful family businesses that exist, there are some 14 million family businesses in the european union. all family businesses have a few things in common: they think and act sustainably, they pass their business down from generation to generation, they have a close bond, a high level of social responsibility towards their workforce, their employees, and they are generally very local. this means that they do not move from one place to another, if the tax laws in one country or another are perhaps a little more favourable. no, they also have a responsibility in their region, they remain in the region and are therefore as important for the local town or municipality as they are for competitiveness in europe. all this stability, renewal and growth in the family business sector ultimately benefits our european economy and the growth we so badly need in the european union. many family businesses are small and medium-sized enterprises, but not all. there are many family businesses with between 500 and 1 000 employees, which unfortunately do not fall under the definition of smes. and yet these larger family businesses have the same problems as smes: they suffer from too much bureaucracy, from complicated tax systems, from too little support. at the same time, they do not benefit from special support for smes. i think it is therefore right that we in this parliament should ask ourselves: if we are to move away from purely quantitative criteria in defining smes, should we not also take more account of qualitative criteria, such as the interlinking of ownership, control and management, risk of liability? in any case, we finally need an eu-wide definition of the concept of family business that is also suitable for the statistical offices in the member states and can be used. family businesses have the same problems almost everywhere in europe. one is the search for a suitable successor, which is often very difficult in many family businesses. statistics say that every year there are about 150,000 companies that have problems, that have to close because they can't find suitable successors. if you convert that into jobs, we're talking about 600,000 jobs lost every year. and of course, family businesses also tend to have a much higher equity ratio than non-family businesses. this is what leads to economic stability for businesses and the economy as a whole. that's why we need to take that into account when we invest. it is no wonder that companies in all member states complain about excessive taxation. equity capital remaining in the region, invested to maintain the business, should be exempted from taxation as far as possible. i would urge the commission to give more attention to family businesses. six years ago there was a working group in the commission devoted to this chapter. nothing's happened since then. i think that if we want growth, prosperity and employment in the european union, as we are aiming to do, then we must take account of the specific features of family businesses and simply ask ourselves: how can we give these family businesses - our backbone, and also the backbone of industry and the economy in the european community - even greater support, how can we help them better to solve their problems? there will be a lot of national-level action. but i think that the comparison of best practices and a clear commitment also at european level to promote and support these our strong family businesses is an honourable thing. that is why i am asking for support for my report tomorrow.
the rapporteur. the commission is not i would like to begin by thanking my co-rapporteur, giulia moi. we have worked together very well and we agree on what we are now putting to the vote in parliament at first reading. we want to make two proposals for directives from the european commission into one single regulation which applies equally in all member states. this is particularly important in a subject as fundamental as cloning. all member states must act in the same way. the common market requires this. our proposal is very consistent. we want to ban cloning altogether, because cloning is animal cruelty. the success rate is extremely low, ten percent, says efsa. this varies by species, but ultimately it's a minimal success. why is that? the cloning technology is not mature, and in the last 12 years or so there has been no progress at all in this technology. mortality rate remains high. animals born alive - the few that are born alive - suffer to a large extent from malformations, malformations of internal organs or of the external extremities, they suffer from immunodeficiency and, for example, from problems of the respiratory tract. as a result, many of these live-born animals die in the first few weeks before they are even laid. and they die in pain. can we let that happen? is it not our responsibility to care for the welfare of animals? as i said, this technique is being used, even though it doesn't work. it is not directly applied in the european union, but in third countries - in north america, i think perhaps also in south america, in china for example - and we benefit from it because we can import so far. we can import reproductive material or clone the offspring of humans. is that right? is it right for us to say: yes, we have nothing to do with cloning technology, it is not used in europe, but we would like to have the reproduction material. this is a trick! we wash our hands of the guilt and let others do the dirty work, but we want to profit from the success. and is it really that successful? as i said, the mortality rate is extremely high. and the progress in breeding is, in our view, extremely limited. because there are biological limits to the animal. at some point, a farm animal's body is also exhausted, and everything else - more and more production, more and more muscle packs on an animal, more and more milk forced on the animal - is ultimately animal cruelty in the farm. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's farmers are not left behind. can we let that happen? the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. that too must be taken into account. the removal and re-implantation of eggs is not without risks, and there are a high number of cesarean sections. finally, there is something that is extremely moving here, something that has always moved the european parliament, as well as our citizens in the european union: it is the fact that every reproductive technology developed for farm animals has finally reached humans. and it is this concern that drives people in the european union. that's why they're against cloning. they don't want to have that because they have that very fear that cloning, if it works properly, will eventually be applied to humans. so, defend the beginners! it actually touches the very roots of our own human existence. our citizens do not want the meat of cloned animals on their plates either. but they may already be being cheered on. that's why we want to ban everything. we want to ban not only the use of cloning technology in the european union but also the import of reproductive material, the import of clones and their offspring. and we want to make labelling compulsory for what may already have been placed on our market. is that unrealistic? we think no. traceability is possible, as the experience of gmos has shown. in the case of feed and food, it was possible to introduce a traceability system for third countries worldwide. and if the european commission now says: 'oh, that is not possible with farm animals', then in our view that is not true. there are breeding books for farm animals. farmed animals are therefore even more traceable by origin. that is our view, and we think that all of this is doable. i would therefore ask the european commission to reconsider the whole thing. and i would ask my colleagues in the house, above all, to give their full support to our joint report - the report by giulia moi and myself. you are doing something for the welfare of animals and you are also doing something for the european union's community of values. we have a responsibility here as members of the european parliament. sometimes politics has to set limits, and today is the day. please help us draw that line! thank you very much.

in writing. ‒ this report implements necessary changes to the existing regulation banning the sale of seal products in the european union to meet wto requirements. this concerns the exemption for the import of seal products from seals hunted for the purpose of sustainable management of marine resources (bmr exemption) and the exemption for the import of seal products from hunting traditionally conducted by inuit and other indigenous communities (gi exemption). following a complaint by canada and norway, the wto decided that the bmr exemption should be removed and the ig exemption should be specified to focus more clearly on the protection of inuit tradition. compliance with wto recommendations and decisions is essential for efficient global trade, and discrimination against individual trading partners is a barrier to free trade. both the commission proposal and the committee report implement wto decisions. they work against discriminatory trade practices without being in conflict with animal welfare. the report is therefore welcome. i agreed to it. i am also of the opinion - and this is my ceterum censeo - that the single euro must be abolished. it is a source of discord and strife in europe.

in writing. ‒ the report i drafted in the committee on agriculture was adopted by a large majority in the plenary. in recent years, more and more rules have been added to the eu's agricultural policy without reducing existing bureaucracy. that has to change.
in writing. ‒ i thank the rapporteur for his very good report, which can make an important contribution to the much needed de-bureaucratisation of the common agricultural policy. the provisions of the cap have become considerably more diverse and complex with the latest reform, despite the commission's announcements to the contrary. the increasing complexity of controls has not only led to increasing error rates, but also to increasing costs. every year, 4 billion euros are spent on checks on the use of agricultural funds alone. the question arises, and rightly so, whether taxpayers' money is being handled responsibly and efficiently. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's agricultural policy is not disrupted by the introduction of new technologies. the number of on-the-spot checks must be reduced urgently. more performance-based controls can relieve farmers who have performed well. in addition, it must be ensured that penalties for errors distinguish between clear fraud and unintentional errors. a farmer who inadvertently places a cross in the wrong place in an application without causing economic damage cannot be sanctioned in the same way as a fraudster who acts deliberately.
in writing. i have agreed with my group to the european parliament resolution on 'protecting the financial interests of the european union: towards performance-based controls of the common agricultural policy'. the report is a step forward towards greater financial and budgetary accountability. it is also about cutting red tape and simplifying processes. this is nowhere more important than in the common agricultural policy, which has been a nucleus of the eu's growing growth over the last few decades and has always been a playground for the clash of national interests. i support anything that lights up the thickness of this area.
