president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the causes of the refugee flows affecting the european union lie in the terrible conflicts in syria and iraq and in the crises that have been going on for a very long time in afghanistan and the horn of africa. the decisions taken by the heads of state or government at their informal meeting on 23 september confirm the european union's strong commitment to the crisis, both internally and externally, and to the humanitarian dimension. in very concrete terms, we are now freeing up the resources needed to be able to refinance humanitarian organizations active on the ground, such as the high commissioner for refugees and the world food programme, to better meet the needs of refugees close to their place of origin, in turkey, jordan, lebanon and iraq. in syria, we remain the largest donor to the country's endless war. we are committed to strengthening the main trust funds to launch concrete projects. this allows us to help refugees in critical areas, such as education and youth employment. i am thinking of course of the madad fund which was suffering from considerable under-funding and the emergency fund for africa. in both cases, this is in response to a joint request from the european parliament and the heads of state or government. at internal level, the council, aware of the scale of the crisis and the urgency of responding effectively and swiftly to the humanitarian situation of refugees, has done its utmost to treat this issue as a matter of the highest priority. for this reason, two extraordinary meetings of the justice and home affairs council were convened on 14 and 22 september 2015, in addition to the meetings already scheduled by the presidency, in order to follow up on the guidelines given by the european council at its meetings in april and june, the european agenda on migration presented by the commission in may and the additional package of measures submitted by the commission on 9 september. as minister for labour and employment, i organized, not later than yesterday, in the framework of the ministerial lunch, an exchange on the support that the european union and the commission can give to the states which are currently hosting the largest number of refugees, to facilitate their integration, to facilitate their access to the labour market, to support language courses, the assessment of their professional qualifications, the schooling of children, etc. commissioner thyssen has given us a number of thoughts on the use of funds, including from the european social fund, to intervene at this level. the presidency intends to continue this reflection, also in the framework of the epsco council, in order to implement an approach in a coherent and solidary manner in the countries which are hosting the largest numbers of refugees. all these efforts have made it possible and must make it possible to achieve important and significant results in the shortest possible time, in particular the adoption on 14 september of a council decision establishing provisional measures in the field of international protection for the benefit of italy and greece, which will allow the relocation of a first contingent of 40 000 refugees. at its meeting on 22 september the council also adopted a second decision for the relocation of 120 000 persons in need of international protection from italy and greece or any other member state which might need it. i am pleased to note that the first hotspots are already operational and i understand that more hotspots will be operational soon. the roadmaps were submitted by italy and greece and have already been presented at the expert forum organised by the commission in collaboration with easo and at the meeting of the strategic committee on immigration, borders and asylum on 5 october. the practical aspects of the implementation of relocation mechanisms were discussed in detail at these meetings. the council welcomes the excellent cooperation with parliament in the examination of these decisions and the responsiveness shown by parliament. this demonstrates the common will to achieve concrete results in providing refugees with the protection and assistance to which they are entitled and member states, especially those most at risk, with the assistance and assistance they require. we also support humanitarian aid to refugees trying to find refuge in the european union when they cross the southern mediterranean, particularly from libya. in this context, i would like to stress that we are counting on very concrete results with our partners at the valletta summit, whether on the root causes of migration, on refugee protection issues, on the fight against human trafficking or on cooperation on return and readmission. ladies and gentlemen, mr president, as the presidency we are actively engaged in mobilising member states and our key partners to achieve our objective of doubling the contribution from the union budget and reaching an additional €1 billion to support the humanitarian organisations involved in this crisis. recently, the netherlands and belgium announced additional contributions of eur 48.5 million and eur 30 million respectively. the united kingdom announced an additional £100 million and france and germany each announced an additional €100 million. these efforts, which put the european union at the forefront, must also be accompanied by the support of the entire international community. in this regard, we welcome the fact that germany, as g7 chair, has just organised an outreach event on the sidelines of the un general assembly ministerial week, which has resulted in commitments of over eur 1.8 billion. as you know, the commission has already put forward proposals for budgetary adjustment, and we, as the presidency, are determined to support this approach in the council. we will of course need the active support of the european parliament for the rapid implementation of the decisions taken and the necessary budgetary adjustments. i'm sure we can count on you in this regard.
first vice-president of the commission. – mr president, today we are all put to the test. we are faced with what is arguably the biggest challenge to europe in a generation. what is being put to the test is our capacity to handle a huge humanitarian crisis. what is being put to the test is our capacity to understand that there will be solutions only at a european level. what is being put to the test is the very fabric of our european union. what is being put to the test is actually the fundamental values we share, and much that was said this morning testifies to this. i have to note that when people try to argue that those arriving in europe today are, in the majority, people seeking a better future, not refugees – which is completely unfounded, there are no scientific data – and people say this in this house, i draw some hope from this because they do not want to be seen not to be doing something for real refugees. my hope is that once those in this house who currently reject everything we do understand that we are actually dealing with a majority of real refugees, they will see the fallacy of their ways and come to the conclusion that there are only european solutions here. there is no need to hide from that fact. i say this also: (interjection from the floor: ‘go to the camps and talk to them’) it is being said here – because this is apparently the way people who disagree with you think they can make a point – it is being said behind me here ‘go and talk to them in the camps’. well, that is exactly what i did. that is exactly what i did, but apparently you only hear what you want to hear when you talk in the camps. i know that, in this day and age, fear is an important factor in european society. many european citizens are afraid, and you know what fear has as a characteristic: when you are afraid you go and look for proof that your fear is justified and you are not open to proof that your fear is unjustified. responsible politics in this situation is not to cater to fear, not to create stereotypes, not to put people in groups, but to come up with solutions to a problem instead of just increasing people’s fears in the hope that it will provide you with more votes at the next election. this is also the time when politicians across europe will be challenged on whether their integrity still prevails or whether they go for the easy solution of catering to fears in the hope of then gaining political position. i hope we will all be responsible in this phase. the european council was responsible last week, by paving the way for decisions that can now be implemented. let me briefly go through them. they decided last week to strengthen external borders and increase the financial and human resources for our agencies, frontex, the european asylum support office (easo) and europol, and to increase funding for the eu home affairs funding programmes, with eur 100 million for emergency assistance to the most affected eu member states. this is in addition to the eur 73 million already exhausted. much of this funding is going to address the immediate humanitarian needs – to help member states provide the necessary shelter, health, welfare and other specific basic needs of new arrivals. we speeded up the preparation of the western balkan conference next thursday. we speeded up the roll-out of support teams in the hotspots in the most affected member states, to identify, register and fingerprint migrants. this is essential to make sure we do indeed distinguish between those who have the right to asylum and those who do not. it was also decided to uphold, apply and implement the existing dublin rules and the schengen acquis; to match the mobilised eu budget contributions with member state contributions, including notably eur 1 billion for the unhcr, the world food programme and other agencies to respond to the urgent needs of displaced syrian refugees in the region; to assist turkey, lebanon and jordan in dealing with the refugee crisis through the help of the trust fund for syria; to increase the funding of the emergency trust fund for africa; and to speed up preparations for the valetta summit on 11—12 november. these are important decisions. let us implement them. the issue here is not that we do not know what to do; the issue is that, as in other areas, we lack self-confidence. we can handle this – i agree with chancellor merkel: ‘wir schaffen das’ – i have no doubts. we need to address the issue of what i would call also in this area ‘moral hazard’. member states need to be able to trust that other member states will do their part. this is the core issue here, that so-called frontline member states will do their part in making sure that our external borders are better controlled and that people who arrive are immediately fingerprinted, and that those member states who are not frontline states will do their part in showing their solidarity with the member states who bear the brunt of the arrivals. there is an issue here of just doing what we agreed, and then the self-confidence in europe will increase, and mutual trust will also increase – and that is what we need between member states. as i said before, winter is coming. i spoke to the high commissioner for refugees, antónio guterres, yesterday and he said clearly that we know how to, and we certainly can, winter-proof the refugee camps, the tents, the reception centres, but we cannot winter-proof masses of people on the move – and moving in an unpredictable and fast manner. you cannot winter-proof movements of people. in geneva yesterday our interlocutors welcomed the latest eu steps to mobilise the budget for these purposes. to name but a few: eur 200 million to the unhcr world food programme and other aid agencies to respond to the urgent needs of displaced persons and refugees in the region; eur 300 million in humanitarian aid next year and, as you know, we asked member states to match this and the heads of state or government agreed to do that. i am looking forward to taking stock of these promises at the next european council and i hope people understand that eur 1 billion of funding is not too much to ask for in humanitarian aid. in this respect, i am again very grateful to this parliament, yet again leading by example and fast-tracking the adoption of the budgetary proposals we made last week. this parliament as an institution has assumed its responsibility in an admirable way. the trust fund for syria, aiming to reach eur 1 billion, was also welcomed by those frontline states that will need to deal with the approaching winter. humanitarian aid is our urgency of today. when it comes to humanitarian aid, it is not enough to find necessary funding. you need to put in place necessary help mechanisms, linking manpower and assets. and those challenges are high on the agenda of my colleagues commissioners avramopoulos, stylianides and hahn, and also commissioner andriukaitis, who is working on the health issues. the civil protection mechanism is ready to be activated. we need to do this quickly. we do not want to waste time. a quantum leap in reception capacities in greece is probably the most urgent priority that we are tackling on a daily basis. president juncker has put in place people to coordinate the national and european technical assistance resources being mobilised to help greece. without reception capacity nothing will work, and we all agree on that. greece will have a separate programme with unhcr on this. this needs to be finalised in the coming weeks. greece needs to return to the dublin system, and i have to say that i salute the greek government for committing to returning to the dublin system. you will not hear me saying that all is ready for winter but this commission has identified and proposed all the operational and budgetary measures that are needed internally within the eu and outside our borders. with regard to turkey, the president has said more than enough: we will continue working on this, and you will also be informed this afternoon about exactly what we will be doing in the next couple of weeks. i think you will agree with me that, while working on the humanitarian situation and sharing the burden with the most affected countries, we should also not neglect the wider issue in relation to managing the situation and the root causes of the situation. the valletta summit will be important – however, i will limit myself to referring to what president juncker has said about that. refugees, on the run from war and persecution, willing to risk everything for even the chance of a decent life, will continue to flee. they simply have no other option. and we have no other option but to provide a safe haven for them, to protect them and to treat them properly, here in the european union, as well as in other countries where they arrive. so it is time to rebuild our self-confidence and our mutual confidence in our ability to deal with this most pressing humanitarian issue effectively, and together wir schaffen das!

in writing. ‒ i agree to the disbursement of funds from the european union solidarity fund (eusf) to greece and bulgaria. natural disasters are random. the eusf was set up to provide solidarity assistance in the event of major natural disasters within the european framework. it is one of the few instruments which is meaningfully located at a supranational level. the eu is thus authorising eur 16.2 million to provide aid for the natural disasters in greece and bulgaria in winter 2015. in greece, five regions were affected by severe flooding, while in bulgaria severe winter weather caused considerable damage. the funds eur 9.9 million for greece and eur 6.3 million for bulgaria are intended to cover part of the costs of emergency aid and reconstruction measures following these natural disasters. the main purpose of the appropriations will be to restore vital infrastructure and services, to reimburse the costs of emergency and rescue operations and to cover part of the costs of clean-up in the affected regions.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the be/ford genk motion. the 'fund for adaptation to globalisation' is a social policy instrument of the european union. at the request of eu member states, workers who have lost their jobs as a result of the effects of globalisation or the global financial crisis can be assisted in finding a new job. the global fund will provide €6.3 million in this case. this money will help the 4 500 former ford genk workers to find new jobs. i welcome the investment in training to help jobseekers find quality jobs.
in writing. ‒ i am voting as my group against any disbursement from the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) on principle so against this too. the egf is intended to help workers who have lost their jobs as a result of changes in the pattern of world trade. the egf shall be managed in accordance with the principle of sound financial management. the fund can cover up to 60% of the cost of projects which can help redundant workers find a new job or start their own business. the egf is only used where more than 500 workers are made redundant by a single undertaking (including suppliers and downstream companies) or where a large number of workers in a single industry are made redundant in one or more neighbouring regions. there is no reason to place these measures at european level. this is contrary to the principle of subsidiarity.

member of the commission.– madam president, honourable members, i am grateful for the opportunity to have this point on the agenda and to explain to you the actions of the commission over the past 10 days, because we face a very difficult case of fraud. let me speak frankly: this is fraud committed by one company and this fraud has put at stake public trust in european cars, and has seriously put at stake the credibility of our legal system and its efficiency in protecting consumers and the environment, which is the backbone of the european union’s actions and regulations. i believe we will be able to overcome it. i thank the european parliament for giving me this opportunity to share information and also – at the very beginning – i want to say that i am ready to continue providing you with every piece of information about my future actions to ensure that such a fraud will not happen again. the commission and member states agreed, at the competitiveness council on thursday 1 october 2015, just last week, to act quickly and to act collectively. this means three things. firstly, investigating and establishing the facts and enforcing the existing rules – which is what all of you are calling for. secondly, accelerating the adoption of the regulatory framework formations. and thirdly, changing the approval and surveillance systems so that this cannot happen again. i will speak about each of these in turn and i want you to know that the commission will play a full role in sorting this out. let me begin with the first point: establishing the facts and enforcing the existing rules. this is the point from where we have to start. we must start by establishing the facts. you ask me how the commission will investigate any potential wrongdoing. the commission does not have the power to carry out our own investigation in the automotive sector. we rely on the authorities of the member states. these institutions are professional. let us not jeopardise what we have built together so far: a widespread feeling of mutual suspicion is not helping coherent and effective european action. in fact, investigations have already been launched in several member states and the commission has encouraged all the others, every member state and every manufacturer, to do the same – i have sent a letter to all of the member states. the commission is providing a platform for the exchange of information between member states, in the sense that we have already convened several meetings of government and type-approval authorities. we have also discussed this matter in detail, as i mentioned before, at the competitiveness council on 1 october 2015. the national authorities are together exchanging information with the commission about this case and the commission is also organising a meeting with the national type-approval authorities that will be held on 15 october 2015. we need, as soon as possible, to have clarification on the extent of the fraud. for instance, the following questions: how many vehicle models are involved; how many vehicles in total; and under which conditions have vehicle sales been banned? and once we have the facts, we must act. as i have stressed several times, we have zero tolerance for fraud. we must send a very clear message today on the enforcement of existing rules, and those rules must be strictly adhered to. here again, national authorities have a very crucial role to play. we need to be clear about what we will do and when we will do it; what actions will be taken to remedy this situation and when they will be carried out. we need to restore consumer confidence as quickly as possible – i think this is where the real damage that has been done – and we need to apply the rules even if that means sanctions. we owe this to europe’s citizens. i have asked member states to work together on this because i think uncoordinated national action will make things even worse. we will only succeed if we act together. on the second point, regarding accelerating the change in the regulatory framework for emissions, the question was whether we noticed that something was wrong. we noticed that the system of testing emissions in laboratories is not the right one, and the commission proposed draft regulations on real-driving emission (rde) testing a few years ago. the first package was voted on in may, but i think we have to accelerate matters. the new legislation will improve the test procedure for directly assessing the regulated emissions of light-duty vehicles under real driving conditions. the new testing procedure will eliminate the possibility of using defeat devices and it will ensure that the regulatory emissions limits are actually met. the second package of the rde procedure, setting out the exact timing and level of what are called conformity factors, is planned to be voted on this year. we will do it. on the third point, improving the approval and surveillance system so this cannot happen again, where should we act at eu level? let me list those areas where action is urgently needed and where full support is essential – including the full support of the european parliament. the existing approval system for motor vehicles in the eu lies with pre-market testing and the approval of vehicles. this is a system that is used almost all over the world, and it has been studied and evaluated in detail for several years. so far, i want to stress ‘so far’, the conclusion of our studies has been that this system has been effective in ensuring safe and environmentally friendly cars on our roads. it has also ensured that the internal market is fully harmonised and that every time a member state authority approves a vehicle type it can be bought and registered in 28 member states. this has obvious advantages for both citizens and industry. our study’s conclusion also indicated that we can improve the system – and this has to be stressed – especially as regards governance and market surveillance. we have therefore been working on a new commission proposal for the last years on the eu type-approval system for motor vehicles. however, in light of the volkswagen problem, and drawing conclusions from what has occurred, we will analyse our proposal again and will suggest further changes that will prevent similar events from happening. i hope to present the proposal to the college of commissioners as soon as possible. it will then be presented to you and to the council, and we expect that our common work will be quick. we expect that the resulting work will contribute to more effective market surveillance, to implementing robust ex-post checks and to improving safeguard measures and recall procedures. let me say it again: european consumers must be reassured that non-confirmed products are not circulated on the eu market. and finally, i have a message to us all. we need to ask ourselves what lesson we can draw from this fraud and this behaviour. we have to remind companies that they should respect the letter and the spirit of the law, because socially and environmentally responsible companies have been one of europe’s biggest assets. i hope that we can work together for this to continue to be the truth.

terrible conflict in syria you just described is now in its fifth year, and at this point there is still little sign of peace on the horizon. that is unfortunately true. a quarter of a million people have been killed; 12 million – half of the country’s population – have been displaced. four million of these have left to lebanon, jordan and turkey, and as europeans we are all aware that many of these refugees are now trying to reach europe in search of peace and a more human life. many are predicting new waves of refugees from inside syria in the months to come. europe has to handle the humanitarian consequences of this conflict, including the flows of refugees. a high-level conference on the eastern mediterranean and western balkans route takes place tomorrow in luxembourg. we have through the new trust fund for syria deals with schools and education. syria is losing a whole generation to war and exile: only education can give a future to a whole country. we expect that, by the not in itself halt the refugee flow from syria: only when there is hope for an end to the war and prospects to return home will the current refugee crisis head towards a conclusion. there is growing consensus in the international community that ending the syrian war needs a two-track approach. this has been verified during a number of meetings over the past two weeks in new york and in brussels. terrorism is one thing – and in syria that means fighting the groups defined as terrorists by the united nations, including daesh and jabhat al-nusra. it does not mean fighting alongside the regime in madam president, just yesterday leyla zana was here in parliament. it was mentioned and everybody who wanted to had the chance to listen to her and her report about the situation in turkey. she was talking about how the freedom of the press is violated, how kurds are under attack and whole kurdish villages are under attack. yet unfortunately, from the commission, from the council and also from the member states we hear very little – surprisingly little – critique of turkey. instead, when erdoğan comes to brussels he is welcomed with full honours, and there is a reason for that. the commission and, it seems, also the council, want to make a dirty deal: they want to make sure that erdoğan stops the refugees who are fleeing from the war in syria towards europe, so that they stay in turkey. the other side of the deal is that president erdoğan gets complete silence from the european arena. i think this deal is wrong. it is not a deal that is worthy of eu values, of human rights and of what we are fighting for. it is not worthy, both because of what it means for refugees and because of what it entails for human rights in turkey. declaring turkey to be a safe country of origin is even more cynical. how can people be safe when journalists are being put in prison? how can minorities be safe in turkey? they simply are not. so, yes to cooperation with turkey, yes to supporting turkey – because it is indeed receiving a lot of refugees – and yes to credible accession negotiations, but no to these dirty deals on the back of refugees.

does the fire-prone internal state of turkey suddenly matter? for years now, we have seen nothing but regression and a departure from european values. it is not a safe third country in my view. the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force. he also says he's been teaching us a lesson in humanity. i think that's bold. is it humane to use war refugees as a means of pressure on the eu? turkey is, after all, largely responsible for the mass influx into europe. the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force, and it is a political force, and it is a political force. and of course people want to go, because there are very few, only a fraction of the two million or so in turkey who are in refugee camps and who are getting basic services. are not many in the country traveling and begging and having to try to make a living doing illegal, low-paying work? the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the situation in turkey is not so bad as it is today. what does erdoğan want? he also wants financial support. that's right, too. i'm also in favor of giving him money. but that's not the point. it's about something else. for example, visa liberalization is also a matter of concern. it is linked to the readmission agreement, which erdoğan is violating by opening the borders to the european union. let me say one more thing: i want to know from the european commission why the presentation of the progress report, which was scheduled for next week, has been postponed. i have heard that this progress report was allegedly leaked to the turkish government in advance and that erdoğan complained about it. but now, because of the desire to be so good to mr erdoğan, this progress report is postponed until easter monday because it is critical. i demand to know!

i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i can say it's a good thing. the european procedure for crossborder small claims already exists. the experience we have had so far has shown that we have been able to reduce the costs for those concerned by 40%. the duration of the procedure was also considerably reduced. this has given us the courage to raise the limit from eur 2 000 to eur 10 000 and the good thing is that with eur 10 000 we will be able to settle 50% of all disputes in this procedure. this is particularly true of citizens and particularly of small and mediumsized enterprises. it's very important to them. i think the big companies, they have legal departments, they can take care of their claim, but it's particularly about the european single market. the small and mediumsized enterprises are particularly affected. and then, if we can come up with some other improvements, we can keep going. this is a good day for the citizens of europe as a whole.
in writing. ‒ the report advocates the extension of the small claims procedure and the european order for payment, which have been in place since 2007, with the aim of making it easier, faster and cheaper to settle disputes in crossborder cases with a small value for money. the procedure is intended to help consumers and small and medium-sized enterprises in particular to enforce their claims and to ensure access to justice. in its 2011 resolution, parliament noted that 'the use of small claims courts remains low in some member states and that more needs to be done in terms of legal certainty, language barriers and procedural transparency. other the commission is proposing to increase the threshold for small claims covered by the european procedure from the current eur 2000 to eur 5000. the new threshold for smes is expected to be a significant improvement. the increase in the threshold proposed by parliament, the council and the commission in the trilogue procedure, the improved use of electronic communications and the limitation of court fees can bring savings and cost savings to both businesses and consumers. i have therefore voted in favour of this report. i am also of the opinion that the single euro must be abolished. it is a source of discord and strife in europe.

in writing. ‒ i voted today in favour of the report on limiting emissions of certain pollutants into the air. as a member of the european parliament for the family party, i am guided by the principle that we have only borrowed the world from our children. i therefore support all measures which help in a practical way to make our economy more sustainable.
in writing. ‒ i have agreed to the report on limiting emissions of certain pollutants into the air. air pollution is a transnational problem requiring action at union level. the proposed amendments to the original legislative proposal will contribute to the reduction of red tape. this would improve air quality across the eu without imposing unjustified burdens on the economy and society.
in writing. ‒ this report focuses on the limitation of emissions of certain pollutants from medium combustion plants. as part of the air quality package, the eu commission presented the proposal for a directive on the reduction of pollution from medium combustion plants in december 2013. the directive is intended to apply to combustion plants with a heat output of up to 50 megawatts; this applies in particular to large buildings as well as small industrial plants. it is proposed to introduce a registration requirement for medium combustion plants and to set emission limit values for pollutants such as sulphur dioxide, nitrogen and particulate matter produced by combustion plants. while small and large combustion plants are regulated, emissions from medium-sized combustion plants are not regulated. there are currently no limit proposals. the commission is working on this. our committee, itre, supports this report for the following main reasons: air pollution is a transnational problem therefore regulation at eu level is necessary. it is intended to fill a significant gap in eu law. according to a commission impact assessment, the health costs of air pollution in europe are estimated at around eur 940 million per year. i voted in favour of this report. i am also of the opinion that the single euro must be abolished. it is a source of discord and strife in europe.

in writing. ‒ i do not agree with the regulation of emissions from combustion plants with a capacity of between 1 and 50 mw. the main reason is that this area has so far been left unregulated by the eu. but two other reasons are also crucial. firstly, it was agreed to exclude combustion plants in the offshore sector and in certain areas such as french overseas. if regulation is so good, it should be universal and equal for all. if the regulation requires exceptions to the scope, then it is bad. it doesn't matter where the air pollution is caused. i have supported the amendments. secondly, the commission is given the power to set the limit values. i think that this is a task which should be left to the legislator. since there are no adequate means of control of the commission by the european parliament, and even less of accountability, i reject the further undermining of the democratic principle, which is already weak at european level.

in writing. ‒ i support the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending the financial regulation applicable to the general budget of the union. the report aims to ensure that eu funds are used in a transparent, efficient and appropriate manner. it also sets out important changes to the financial regulation, which are necessary, inter alia, to take account of the new directive on public procurement and concession contracts.
in writing. ‒ in the report we proposed to amend regulation (eu, euratom) no 966/2012 on the financial regulation applicable to the general budget of the union as follows: new provisions are to be introduced, such as market consultancy, the new innovation partnership as a procedure, the introduction of compliance with environmental, social and labour law as an essential condition, the evaluation of the criteria in no particular order, a pricing methodology based on the most economically advantageous offer. in addition, concessions for works and services are introduced for the first time in the financial regulation and are subject to the same types of procedures as public contracts. the reasons for exclusion and the possibility of the remedies concerned shall be clearly stated. exclusions are clearly separated from rejection of a particular procedure to avoid confusion. the purpose of the system is to ensure the early detection and prevention of risks and the publication of information on an excluded economic operator, in order to protect the interests of the eu. i have therefore voted in favour of this report. i am also of the opinion that the single euro must be abolished. it is a source of discord and strife in europe.

mr president of the french republic, ladies and gentlemen, first of all, allow me, on behalf of the european parliament, mr president, to express our condolences and solidarity with you after the floods which caused the death of 20 french and european people and devastated the alpes-maritimes last weekend. our thoughts are with the victims and their families.
mr president of the republic, madam chancellor, i welcome you both to the european parliament. the fact that you - the french president and the german chancellor - are speaking together today about the future of europe in the european parliament in strasbourg, the symbol of franco-german reconciliation, and in this house of european democracy is certainly a historic moment. for centuries, your two countries, germany and france, were arch enemies, trapped in a spiral of war, defeat, humiliation and revenge. it was only after millions of lives had been lost and europe had been devastated that the leaders of our two countries, charles de gaulle and konrad adenauer, succeeded in bringing about reconciliation between germany and france. this was a step towards peace in europe - a peace from which we all benefit to this day. without the reconciliation between germany and france, europe could not have grown. but one thing is certain: without european unification, this franco-german friendship would never have existed in its present form. millions of people have found friends and homes in each other's countries through the exchange between our countries.
mr president of the french republic, madam chancellor, you are the first heads of government from your countries to speak together in this house since helmut kohl and françois mitterrand spoke in the european parliament 26 years ago. we welcome it, and it is essential, in these difficult times, difficult times for europe, when unprecedented challenges await us, that you have come to strasbourg to debate with us, the representatives of the peoples. the last few decades have taught us that when franco-german cooperation fails, the whole of europe suffers. it was not good understanding or unity that brought europe forward but contradictory ideas and divergent opinions, because, once france and germany agree, the negotiations, however tough, usually lead to a good compromise that takes advantage of the strengths of both for the benefit of all the partners and the union as a whole. that is why, mr president, madam chancellor, we are now anxious to hear what your ideas are and what impetus you intend to give to our common future. i give the floor to the president of the french republic, françois hollande.

broke down walls, freed peoples, gave nations hope. the european parliament has been a great help to the people of europe, and it is a great help to the people of europe, and it is a great help to the people of europe. and it is the whole of europe that has thus been built up with considerable hope. the common conviction of françois mitterrand and helmut kohl was to build a political union of europe, thus extending the mandate of the founders, to create a vast single market with social rules, and to carry the project of a common currency. all this had to be part of the same process and be carried out with the same determination. today, 26 years later, chancellor angela merkel and i are addressing you. firstly, because it is the 25th anniversary of german reunification, but above all because europe is experiencing new tragedies which pose new challenges to our continent. in fact, for years europe has been facing a succession of crises: the financial crisis, which originated outside our continent but has spread and has caused an economic crisis from which we are barely emerging and a social crisis, with millions of young people out of work. now, this is a humanitarian crisis that we are facing with an influx of refugees, caused by the destabilization of entire regions in the middle east, in africa, resulting from armed conflict and with the resurgence of religious hatred. i am not forgetting the security crisis, with a war not so far away, on the borders of europe, in ukraine, and then also the terrorist attacks that have affected several countries of our continent, including my own. with every crisis, fears are manifested. you must live with fear, but you must not live dominated by fear. nevertheless, there is a temptation to withdraw nationally whenever there is a test. but nothing is more futile than trying to escape alone, to hide, to take shelter when major events are happening around the world. we must speak from experience, as history tells us and confirms. these questions may be sincere, but they cannot condemn europe to a state of frivolity and impotence. on the contrary, they justify an offensive europe, capable of both ensuring the protection due to its citizens and maintaining its position in accordance with its interests and values, values which have justified the unification of our continent. there is therefore no other solution than a strong europe to guarantee our own sovereignty. in recent years, in recent months, france and germany have wanted to react together to the trials we have been going through in the last period. we have responded by affirming simple and clear principles: solidarity, responsibility and firmness. solidarity in the face of terrorism, because every attack in one of our countries is directed against the whole of europe: its ideals, its culture, its way of life. it is the soul of our continent. and i thank the heads of state or government, but also many members of the european parliament who met in paris on 11 january to show their solidarity and their commitment to freedom, to what we stand for, to defend us against terrorism which seeks to destroy the very cement that unites us. fighting for its development and precisely to avoid population movements. let's face it, you know? we are facing the exceptional arrival of women and men since the beginning of the year. 600,000, i in writing. ‒ i support my colleague's report on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on payment services in the internal market, amending directives 2002/65/ec, 2013/36/eu and 2009/110/ec and repealing directive 2007/64/ec. the creation of an internal market for payments and electronic transactions makes an important contribution to the protection of consumers in the eu. more and more work is being done across borders and on the internet. the lack of a clear legal framework leads to legal uncertainty and a lack of consumer protection.
in writing. ‒ this proposal is the final confirmation of the compromise reached in july in the trilogue between the ep, the council of ministers and the commission. it builds on a previous directive, 2007/64/ec, and thus completes the framework for a common market for electronic payments. this includes the opening of the market for so-called payment initiation services and account information services. in this respect, the proposal is innovation-friendly, promotes competition between payment service providers and is another building block towards a well-functioning european single market. this common regulation establishes the 'level playing field' in a transparent manner. that is why i am voting in favour of this report. i hereby call on the commission, the ecb and eba to pay careful attention to the following aspects when implementing the directive and subsequently as supervisory authorities: - data protection and security against unauthorised access are non-negotiable and must be guaranteed in all circumstances. - the account information service uses strong customer authentication for account queries. - the third party service must be provided with insurance cover which ensures full compensation of the credit institution holding the account for any damage. i am also of the opinion that the single euro must be abolished. it is a source of discord and strife in europe.

the need for genuine european solidarity to be fully realised. i think that in the last few weeks things have developed in a positive way. the european council has been concerned with this subject since the beginning of the crisis. president tusk spoke to you about it last week. the european council must not only decide on emergency measures, but also develop political guidelines on the whole of migration and asylum policy. tomorrow he will discuss three fundamental aspects. firstly, cooperation with third countries to prevent migratory flows. secondly, to strengthen the protection of the union's external borders. thirdly, to respond to the flow of refugees into europe and to ensure a return policy. let me explain these three aspects in detail. first, cooperation with third countries. mr president, i would first of all like to endorse, on behalf of the presidency and the council, what you said earlier. the murderous and criminal attack that took place in ankara has shocked and upset us all. we are of course with the turkish people, we share their grief and we express our sympathy, solidarity and deepest condolences. but, moreover, we also share what you said about the importance of dialogue, about all the efforts that must be made to organise the elections, to give turkish democracy the strength it so badly needs in these difficult times. i would like to return to the aspect of cooperation with third countries, in particular with countries of origin and transit, which is a top priority for the proper management of migration flows. until conditions in these countries improve, too many refugees will risk their lives to leave and nothing will stop them. on 8 october the high-level conference on the eastern mediterranean and western balkans route was held. it marks the beginning of a process which will enable us to strengthen cooperation with all our partners, in the interests of all, for a more efficient management of migration flows. solidarity with the balkan countries seems to me to be of the utmost importance in this respect. these countries also face difficulties, including economic ones, and we must help, support and sustain them. the valletta summit with african countries, scheduled for mid-november, will have to forge a stronger partnership and lead to concrete measures. a few weeks ago, we had a discussion here in brussels about development, about all aspects of development and also about migration, especially from africa. we must be aware that development and migration are often two sides of the same coin, the coin of underdevelopment and poverty. these two major meetings are tangible proof of the union's determination to engage in constructive dialogues with the countries most concerned. the strengthening of relations with turkey will also be on the agenda of the european council, with a view to the adoption of the joint action plan which we have already discussed, i believe, last week in strasbourg. the second component is the reinforcement of the protection of the union's external borders. the treaty is very clear: we must gradually establish an integrated system for the management of external borders. the european council will endeavour to provide concrete guidance in this respect for the member states, which are responsible for protecting their national borders, but also for the european agencies, in particular frontex, whose tasks in this field should be reviewed and strengthened. thirdly, the response to the flow of refugees into europe and the return policy. we have a duty to help refugees, but among those who cross our borders illegally, we know that not all of them need international protection under the geneva convention. a coherent, credible and effective return policy for illegally staying third-country nationals, which fully respects the human rights and dignity of the persons concerned and the principle of non-refoulement, is an essential element of an overall european union migration policy. this is done first by identification and registration. in this context, the first hot spot was set up in italy. we must of course continue along this path. much remains to be done, particularly with the active support of the member states. the decisions taken in the council on relocation are being implemented and must be implemented to the end. another aspect of our migration and asylum policy will be discussed tomorrow: the external aspect. as many have said, the causes of these human tragedies that produce these migratory phenomena must be eradicated. we need to look actively at our role on the international stage and at what is happening in syria and libya. these issues will also be on the agenda of the european council. ladies and gentlemen, mr president, the presidency has ensured that the council is working tirelessly on the answers to one of the great crises we are going through. we have achieved important and significant results in an extremely short time, including the adoption in september of decisions on the basis of the commission's proposal to relocate 160 000 refugees. more recently, on 8 october, the council adopted conclusions on the future of return policy, which give a clear overview of the work to be undertaken. the council also had a thorough discussion on the management of the union's external borders; it has adopted financial measures to enable policies to be followed up by rapid action on the ground. the ministers of the interior were also informed of the latest developments in the implementation of the relocation decisions and welcomed the first relocation operation which took place on 9 october. my colleague, mr asselborn, the minister for immigration, visited italy and greece on this occasion. in conclusion, i would like to express once again our gratitude for the responsibility that the european parliament has taken on the issue of migration, in particular for the decisions on relocation. in writing.– in the first half of 2015, more than 82 000 migrants from the western balkans applied for asylum in germany. these migrants come from eu candidate or potential candidate countries that have a clear european perspective. we need to ensure that the right to seek asylum is respected for those in need of protection, while especially swift and effective return, readmission and reintegration policies for those who do not qualify for protection are put in place. to resolve the migration crisis for now and the future, the eu needs to agree on a joint migration and asylum policy. this policy should set one european procedure for asylum seekers and refugees, ending the discrepancies between national asylum policies. it should include one permanent and binding mechanism that ensures the fair sharing of responsibility to host asylum seekers and refugees, according to each state’s economic and social capacities. an agreement on a joint european list of safe countries of origin will relieve asylum systems and discourage further economic migrants. we have to stop the inflow of asylum seekers from the western balkans. the european union needs to focus its asylum and reception capacities on those who are truly in need of protection.

president of the council. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would first like to thank you for asking the president to take part in the debate you wanted to have on the consequences of the court's judgment last week. it will of course be up to the commission in the first instance to inform you of its intentions for the coming months. this is not just a matter for the commission, it is a matter for the council and it is also a matter for the member states and the citizens of europe in the first place. let's not forget them. let me first acknowledge that parliament has regularly raised the shortcomings in the transfer of data from the union to the united states under the safe harbour agreement. even before the snowden revelations, parliament had expressed its concerns about the level of data protection and had asked for the suspension of the agreement until its flaws had been corrected. the court of justice has just declared the commission's adequacy decision on the security sphere invalid. it clearly considered that this decision did not offer sufficient protection of the processing of personal data of european citizens. the consequences of this judgment must be carefully analysed, including by the council. the commission presented a first assessment of its potential consequences at the justice and home affairs council meeting on 9 october. the court's judgment concerns a commission decision. it is therefore primarily for the commission to draw the consequences of the court's invalidation of its decision, and i am sure that the commissioner will do so. the judgment also clarifies the powers of the european supervisory authorities when data is transferred to third countries on the basis of an adequacy decision. it is important that the commission works closely with these authorities to ensure that the judgment is interpreted and applied in a uniform manner. in the meantime, citizens need to be reassured that their data is protected. in addition, companies need to be informed about other legal possibilities for data transfers to the us, in the light of the court's judgment. in the longer term, the commission will have to decide what should succeed the decision on the security sphere which has just been invalidated. the answer to this question will have to be found in close dialogue with the american authorities. whatever formula is adopted to succeed the security area decision, it will have to fully respect the court's judgment. while respecting the principles laid down by the court, the commission will be able to take account of the importance for the economy of a regular and legal flow of data between the united states and the european union. ladies and gentlemen, madam president, the court of justice has pointed out that any instrument of the european union must respect a high level of protection of personal data and be in conformity with the charter of fundamental rights, particularly when such data is transferred to third countries. in this context, the council and the european parliament must continue their work on a new robust data protection framework, with the aim of concluding the negotiations by the end of this year. i believe that with this judgment the completion of this reform before the end of the year is all the more urgent and necessary.
member of the commission.– last week’s ruling in the schrems case reaffirmed the importance of data protection as a fundamental right in the eu, including when personal data is transferred to third countries. the commission respects that ruling and will abide by it, as must all stakeholders. the court has declared the 2000 safe harbour decision invalid, and it can no longer serve as a legal basis for transatlantic data transfers. there can be no ‘business as usual’ approach. immediate steps have to be taken to ensure compliance with the ruling. these are: that citizens need to be assured that their personal data will be protected; and that european businesses needing to transfer personal data to the us need guidance about the remaining legal ways of doing so, with appropriate safeguards and the conditions to be fulfilled. the commission is working closely with the european data protection supervisors in working party 29. we want to ensure clear guidance so that we avoid fragmentation in the internal market. there were good first discussions at technical level last week, and this will continue in the plenary tomorrow, which i will also attend. the commission is also in dialogue with business on this issue. today, together with vice-president ansip and commissioner oettinger, i met a delegation of business representatives to hear their practical concerns and to stress the need to comply with the ruling swiftly. they are worried about fragmentation, and they need guidance as a matter of urgency. i want to use the opportunity of this discussion today to assure you that my objective remains a renewed and robust arrangement for transatlantic data flows, taking into account the requirements set out by our highest court. the us side also needs to address these requirements in its own legal order and in practice. after my first discussions with secretary of commerce penny pritzker, i remain confident that this is possible. i am encouraged by reform steps such as the usa freedom act and the draft judicial redress bill, which specifically addresses the situation of eu citizens. but we will be clear in our discussions with the us partners: we need guarantees that the right to data protection is respected when data is transferred to the us. our benchmark is the court ruling. we will immediately resume and step up discussions with the us, building on the work done so far. i will myself go to washington in mid—november to discuss the issue further with my counterparts there. this is an ongoing debate in the us, as it is in europe. i would therefore ask you too, as members of the european parliament, to engage with your counterparts in the us congress on this issue and to be a partner in this. this is important for our wider relationship with the united states of america, our key strategic partner both politically and economically. i want a more informed debate about this process and i see you as an essential partner in this process. i will keep you regularly informed about the next stages of these discussions.

in writing. ‒ the report on the council position on draft amending budget no 6/2015 of the european union for the financial year 2015 is a revision of the estimates of traditional own resources, vat and gni bases and that it results in a change in the distribution of contributions to the union budget between the member states. two new budget lines are established: support expenditure for trust funds managed by the commission in the policy areas of development and cooperation and enlargement, which shall be marked with a reminder; a change in the establishment plan of the berec office, without any change in the total number of posts and in the budgetary appropriations. the member states' contributions to the budget will be reduced by eur 2,26 billion compared to the original 2015 budget, as a result of traditional own resources (i.e. customs duties and sugar levies) exceeding the expected revenue by eur 1 133,5 million. i have therefore voted in favour of this report. i am also of the opinion that the single euro must be abolished. it is a source of discord and strife in europe.

in writing. ‒ i have agreed to use the flexibility instrument. at a time of increasing immigration of refugees to europe, it is crucial that the european union remains responsive and shows that it can respond adequately to a constantly changing situation. since it is not possible to reallocate appropriations due to certain ceilings of the individual budget lines, part of the funds of the flexibility instrument must be used to provide financial assistance. the use of this instrument is expected to amount to eur 66,1 million in 2015 and to a further eur 52,9 million in 2016. this appropriation is intended to cover the financing of the european schools in the member states and the european schools in the union.
in writing. ‒ council regulation (eu, euratom) no 1311/2013 of 2 december 2013 establishing the multiannual financial framework for the years 2014-2020 allows the mobilisation of the flexibility instrument to finance specific expenditure which could not be incurred within the ceiling of one or more headings of the multiannual financial framework. in accordance with article 11 of council regulation (eu) no 1311/2013 and point 12 of the interinstitutional agreement of 2 december 2013 between the european parliament, the council and the commission on budgetary discipline, on cooperation in budgetary matters and on sound financial management, the commission proposes to mobilise the flexibility instrument after having examined all the options for reallocating appropriations under the heading 'security and citizenship' (heading 3) and after having exhausted the remaining margin. the mobilisation concerns an amount of eur 66,1 million, exceeding the ceiling of heading 3 of the multiannual financial framework, to finance measures to deal with the refugee crisis. the payment appropriations corresponding to this proposed mobilisation of the flexibility instrument shall be eur 52,9 million in 2016 and eur 13,2 million in 2017. i have therefore voted in favour of this report.

i have to say that i am not in favour of this. the commission has already made a number of proposals. today is the first time we've discussed concrete legislation since the luxleaks affair. that is why i think this is a very important debate, because it is about sending a clear signal here as a parliament, for clarity, for transparency, for fair tax competition in the european union. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the tax authorities in the member states are able to provide the information required for the tax assessment of a taxable person. i would like to start this debate by expressing my gratitude to the commission, and in particular to the commissioner for competition, for addressing the issue of fair tax competition from the point of view of state aid. because that's all it is in the end. that is why we must do something about it. the commission has put forward a proposal to make all tax rulings with crossborder implications available to the member states in an automatic procedure. i think this proposal by the commission is a good first step. but we have also made a clear statement in the economic and monetary committee in favour of including a wide range of measures. i would like to mention just a few key words: scope. we have advocated that, within the scope of the procedure, all valid tax rulings, in so far as they do not concern natural persons i.e. legal persons , should be included in this procedure. so all tax rulings for legal entities, a significant expansion! we have advocated that the information be exchanged immediately, not every three months as the commission has proposed. we have also asked for additional information to be included here: a tax identification number, deviating tax rates, information where deviations from the normal tax law are applied, and so on. we have explicitly stated that the commission can also use this information in the context of competition law. we consider this to be a very important point, because it is the only way we can exert pressure so that tax law is not applied against the member states or against neighbouring countries, but that everyone is aware that they must also deal with the competition and aid rules when they adopt a tax ruling. i am disappointed - and i want to make this very clear - that the council agreed on 6 october to a proposal which falls far short of what the commission has proposed. the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the taxation of savings income in the event of tax evasion. the council remains unclear. the commission is proposing to postpone the entry into force of the directive for another year. the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the taxation of savings income. i'm disappointed in that. i would like to make it very clear that the finance ministers of the member states have not fulfilled the promise, which was repeatedly given here in parliament, in the special committee and in the economic and monetary committee, to contribute to clarity and transparency. that is why i urge the member states to engage in serious negotiations with the european parliament here in order to achieve the best possible result, namely that we arrive at a clear, transparent european model in the field of tax rulings and tax pricing agreements, which does not make tax law a burden on the neighbour, but ensures that each person is taxed according to his capacity where value is created. i am glad that this has found broad support in the committee and i hope that it will also find broad support in the plenary.
member of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, aggressive tax planning has become a major concern within the eu and at the global level, particularly in the context of the work of the oecd and the g20. increasing transparency of tax returns between the tax authorities of the member states is an important - i would even say major - step in the fight against aggressive tax planning and tax evasion. the decisions taken by the commission last week in the case of fiat in luxembourg and starbucks in the netherlands are in line with this. the cooperation i have with mrs vestager and her services is excellent. member states now have a margin of appreciation to decide whether an advance ruling in tax matters may be relevant in another eu country, this is called the exchange of information on demand. this lack of transparency in tax records is exploited by some companies to artificially reduce their tax contributions! it has become simply intolerable for our fellow citizens who have been called upon to contribute heavily to resolving deficits during the crisis and who have a civic attitude. that is why we put forward an ambitious proposal in march 2015 to introduce an automatic exchange of information on tax returns between all member states. i would like to thank mr ferber for the quality of his report on this proposal. we have always had fruitful discussions on this subject. the member states reached a compromise on 6 october, a political agreement which i believe is quite appropriate, given that the day before we had the publication of the oecd beps recommendations, which were then adopted by the g20 in lima in the framework of the imf meetings. i agree with mr lamassoure, who is still chairman of the special committee on taxation, that parliament's work in this area has exerted - and i thank you on behalf of all the committees - decisive pressure on the member states to reach an agreement. parliament was not at the ecofin council table, but the spirit of parliament was reflected in its decisions. this political agreement - it must be taken as it is - is a strong, strong signal from the european union: it has enabled us to present in lima a common and ambitious european union front for greater tax transparency, and i was able to encourage our partners at the g20 meeting to do the same and to turn this european initiative into a global or world standard. mr ferber expressed disappointment, which was somewhat mitigated by mrs ferreira, and i would like to respond to that. of course, you have raised three points: first, the desire to go beyond crossborder tax returns to encompass all tax returns, secondly, a regret that the retroactivity period was not longer and, finally, a nuance about the fact that we could have gone faster in the implementation of this text. the commission does not disagree with you, mr rapporteur. it is true that the commission's initial proposal went further than what was adopted by the council, but ladies and gentlemen, you know how the council works. the procedure is very complicated, decisions on taxation must be adopted unanimously, and in this case we did so not only unanimously but very quickly, since it took seven months between the submission of the commission's proposal and the adoption of this text by the ecofin council, and the commission agreed to this compromise. why would you do that? because we feel that the main principles of our proposal are retained in this text, including the automatic exchange of tax records, including the broad scope covered, including the exchange of information between all the member states, including the involvement of the commission and this has been discussed at one time or another. there is a good deal of retroactivity, ten years would have been better in my eyes than five, but five - forgive me for the lappiness as we say in french - were better than the three years that were offered to us at one time and that would have begun to be problematic. finally, there is the implementation timetable. i had hoped that the text could enter into force by the end of the first quarter of 2016, but the states argued - which is not entirely wrong, to be honest - the time limits for transposition and voting of such texts. in the end, i would say that this is a reasonably ambitious compromise which does not lead to - it was essential to me and to the commission, and i can assure you that we would not have agreed to anything else - to distort our proposal; it is a compromise of good quality, which marks a very significant step. i would like to stress that the commission's involvement was maintained in the compromise text. i think this is good news for the commission, but also for the general interest and for the european parliament, because this involvement is essential to monitor the functioning of the directive, it increases the credibility of the commitment of the member states, and it is fully supported, i know that by you, the european parliament, and i wanted to thank you for that. if we had remained in a pure exchange between member states, without the involvement of the commission, the risk - how to say - that the administrations would work together not in collusion but with sometimes some accommodation could not have been totally eliminated. let me say a few words about the other two reports we are discussing today. firstly, the agreement signed on 27 may between the european union and switzerland on the automatic exchange of financial information is a historic agreement which marks - and i believe that for our fellow citizens, it is extremely symbolic - the end of swiss banking secrecy for residents of the union. this is a major step in the fight against tax evasion, in line with the objective of ensuring fairer taxation for our citizens. i am glad that the rapporteur, mr kofod, shares this analysis in his motion for a resolution in favour of the conclusion of the agreement and i would of course urge this house, your parliament, to follow the opinion of the committee on economic and financial affairs and to give its full support to this initiative. we also proposed the repeal of the provisions of the savings tax directive, as the measures of the directive on the automatic exchange of financial data adopted at the end of 2014 will come into force from next january. i have some experience in this area, having been minister of finance in a previous life not so far away. firstly, it is regrettable that the savings tax directive was adopted so late that it became obsolete immediately after its adoption. this should be a lesson to us that we must act quickly and decisively in this matter, but it turns out that the new standard goes beyond what the savings tax directive could bring about and so i welcome the report by mrs scott cato, whom i thank, which advocates the withdrawal of this directive. i would like to make a small point, and she will understand it: i think that the way you have spoken about the president of the commission, jean-claude juncker, is a little hasty, and i will rely on what the taxe committee will say, which, i recall, has heard the president who has come to explain himself to it. i think that when you speak of the head of such an important institution, there are words that you have to be able to master and adjust. the commission will report to the council and parliament on the effectiveness of the measures it is required to present on the operation of the automatic exchange of information on the basis of the obligations laid down by the directive on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation. in the meantime, the commission will not fail to take advantage of the opportunities provided by the structured dialogue with parliament and its committee on economic and financial affairs to inform the members of your institution without delay of any significant developments. in short, i think that we are discussing today a major and innovative approach. i call it the transparency revolution: there is public pressure, there is the evolution of technology and the media, but also the role of your parliament, the will of the commission and the fact that the member states are also feeling obliged to act. i am convinced that with our joint action - and we thank the rapporteurs and the various parliamentarians once again - this revolution of transparency will not stop. i would add that the political will of the commission - and mine in particular - is to continue to move forward resolutely during the five years of this commission's mandate. i am also thinking of the principle of effective taxation, which means that the profits of companies, particularly multinational companies, should be taxed where they are created, and of the relaunch of the accis/cctb project, which is important both for transparency and for economic efficiency. i am thinking, finally, of the
