member of the commission.– madam president, i would like to start by thanking the rapporteur ms zuber for this comprehensive report on child poverty. we have taken note of your analysis and we do share your concerns about the high levels of child poverty in many of our member states. as you have pointed out, the risk of poverty and social exclusion is greater for children than for adults. child poverty is a multifaceted issue that demands an integrated and – to the extent possible – preventive approach, looking at both the employment situation of the household and also the rights of the child. the fight against child poverty has been high on our agenda. in 2013, the commission proposed the recommendation ‘investing in children: breaking the cycle of disadvantage’, which is currently being implemented by member states. the commission will keep working to ensure the full operationalisation of this recommendation. in this respect we take note of your suggestion to have a three-pillar approach: access to resources, services and children’s participation. we are also monitoring child-poverty related aspects in the context of the european semester. in its 2013 recommendation, the commission suggested that the best way to support parents and their children is through progressive universalism, which is a system of strong universal services and benefit rights topped up with targeted instruments for particularly disadvantaged groups, such as the roma. the recommendation calls on the member states to provide parents with access to resources, in the form of paid work and adequate family and child benefits, and to high-quality services such as early childhood education and care, health and housing. an integrated approach is key to ensuring children have the best start in life. the commission has also been regularly monitoring the member states’ progress towards the barcelona targets to improve access to childcare. good-quality childcare services have been shown to support the cognitive and social development of children, especially those from low-income backgrounds, and improve their academic and labour market opportunities later on in life. these services are therefore key to reducing the intergenerational transmission of poverty. many member states have made good efforts to improve the provision of these services, but progress is still slow and uneven. we are providing country-specific recommendations to many member states where needed. in 2014 and 2015 many member states received country-specific recommendations to improve income support for families, to expand childcare, as well as to make education more inclusive and to reduce financial disincentives for parents to enter employment. as far as creating a new financial instrument in this area is concerned, we would like to recall that there are already funding opportunities for children in the current european structural and investment funds: the european social fund, the european regional development fund, and others. these instruments have been, in fact, significantly strengthened for the current 2014-2020 programming period. member states should make further efforts to use them to their full potential. in addition, member states have agreed that 25.6% of the european social fund allocation of eur 86 billion is to be earmarked for social inclusion measures, of which eur 8 billion is set aside for access to children’s and childcare services and for measures fighting against early school leaving. in this regard, it is important that all key stakeholders at national, regional and local level are mobilised and form strong partnerships. the european union funds are also supporting healthy nutrition for children. with the european union school fruit scheme, eur 150 million will support the distribution of fruit and vegetables in schools for 2015 and 2016. with these funds we can reach 12 million children across 25 member states. in addition, there is national or private co-funding, estimated to amount to around eur 32 million. all these financial interventions are extremely important for preventing and breaking the intergenerational transmission of poverty and social exclusion. as you know, the commission is currently working on a european pillar of social rights to foster upward convergence of employment and social performance in the european union. we want to ensure that our legislation and policy framework is in line with the realities of modern life – teleworking, digital work, combining work and family duties – and keeps pace with developments in the fast-changing labour market, adequately addressing needs and challenges arising from diverse and innovative forms of work, and that it invests in people through a modernised social framework for those in and out of work. we are also preparing a fresh start for working parents and caregivers. we believe that this new approach will reap benefits for all; in particular, for working parents and other caregivers who seek a better balance to their work and life commitments, but also for women, to support their participation in the labour market. finally, as the employment status of parents is one of the key determinants of child poverty, this initiative will contribute to reducing the number of children who live in households at risk of poverty. let me assure you once again that this commission is committed to addressing child poverty across the european union by restoring economic growth and upward social convergence, fostering job creation and ensuring social fairness. these are not mere abstract concepts. for the 40% of children in some of our member states who live in households at risk of poverty, we need to come with effective solutions to foster employment of their parents and to ensure their full participation in society.
in writing. i support the resolution because we must send a clear signal against child poverty and its social exclusion. unfortunately, child poverty is widespread in the eu even in germany. poverty is not just a matter of money to meet basic needs such as food, clothing and shelter. child poverty is also associated with social exclusion and lack of access to quality education and health services. children are our future, and it is our responsibility to provide them with free access to quality education. the eu is one of the strongest economies on earth, and there can be no excuse for children to be malnourished in any of our member states.
rapporteur.– madam president, first of all i would like to thank all the shadow rapporteurs, the great civil—society organisations and everyone else who has contributed to making this report what it is: a great starting point for making the right changes to european cohesion policy in order to make it more inclusive for marginalised communities – or, as commissioner crețu put it last week, to make the inclusion of marginalised communities one of the priorities for eu cohesion policy. this report is made for people who very often do not have a lobby in this parliament and in eu institutions. it is made for people who are very often overlooked and overheard when it comes to the distribution of eu funds. in the preparation of this report, i have seen examples of where this is still happening today in the european union. in my hometown, gelsenkirchen, i visited a school where i met two girls – two sisters, denise and michaela, 10 and 12 years old – who had recently moved from romania to gelsenkirchen. i met them in their class. they were curious, they wanted to learn, and they were really trying to get integrated into the school in gelsenkirchen. but the question that came up in my head was: will denise and michaela have the same chances and opportunities that i had when i was growing up in gelsenkirchen? will they have the same access to resources i had? when we look at the situation of denise and michaela, there are challenges that they are facing, because very often they are being discriminated against or they are facing structural exclusion. this report can give the tools to cities such as gelsenkirchen to create an integrated approach in order to give a chance to children like this, be it in education or with regard to housing, employment or health. we need to look at different fields of society in order to give a chance to people from marginalised communities. at the same time, we have to bring all the stakeholders together, be they from the local level, from civil society or the people affected themselves, in order to create the best programmes and to really make sustainable investments. and we need to give support for them to have a strong voice in the whole process – not only in the preparation, but also in the monitoring and evaluation, of the programmes. secondly, we simply cannot afford to live in segregated societies, because in the long run, inequality and exclusion is much more expensive for us than inclusion and integration. this is why we need to make sure that eu funds actually reach the people that need them the most. this report will give a very clear signal to both the commission and the member states to do exactly that. be it community-led local development or strong implementation of the partnership principle, or be it monitoring our evaluation mechanisms that need to be improved, we have these tools and we need to implement them in order to make eu funds more inclusive. lastly, alongside the set of good measures and proposals that are in this report, we also need to speak very clearly about the problems. let us not shy away from clearly mentioning the obstacles that we are still facing to have inclusive societies in the european union. be it corruption or fraud, be it the lack of political will or anti-gypsyism, we need to name these barriers in order to create good implementation and overcome these problems. human rights are the basis of the european union. let us mainstream human rights in all policy fields in this parliament and make them also the basis of our work with regard to eu structural funds, because in the end, this is going to create societies where everybody has a chance and can live equally. i want to thank again everyone who has contributed to this report and i hope that it will find your support tomorrow in the vote.

i have to say that i am not in favour of this. the commission is not i would like to thank all those involved who have helped to bring this larger and longer-lasting project to a successful conclusion. the commission has also been very constructive in the negotiations between the council and parliament on insurance mediation. we have taken at least three and a half years, and if, after today's adoption, the directive is implemented in all the member states in 24 months, then we have also successfully completed this aspect of financial market regulation. i would like to thank you for your work, but i would also like to mention the ten most important points. firstly, the scope of the directive, which provides for exceptions for small insurances and for intermediary services. we've been arguing about this for a long time. we have chosen a pro-rata approach and a flat rate. i think that is a reasonable way of doing things in the field of application. secondly, the registration. insurance companies are responsible for ensuring that their insurance distributors register properly. the commission will also be able to provide the necessary information to the competent authorities of the member states in order to ensure that the information is made available to the public. the third point is the qualification requirements. contrary to what some member states have advocated until recently, the qualification in the home member state is decisive for the first registration and not the one in which one has to go. but in the case of continuing training, the member state in which you are employed has a certain say. it was hotly debated. the training obligation has been slightly reduced, but better than nothing. and the member states have the opportunity to check that too. the fourth area is the prohibition of commissions, which has been sought, again from parts of parliament. there is no general prohibition on commissions or obligation to disclose the amount of remuneration. the very different structures of insurance markets have therefore given member states several possibilities to impose stricter information requirements, until the provision of prohibitions on commissions was opened up. this was a council demand which we could not refuse. the fifth point is the product information sheet, which is part of our catalogue of measures to improve consumer protection. there's been a long resistance here. the commission has also examined the possibility of a simplified product information sheet, which would be a standard format for eiopa to propose. the sixth point is product overview and management. the rules for product supervision and management have been introduced for all insurance products, following the example of the markets and financial instruments directive. the risk is that if eiopa is not restrained in this matter, it will end up as a bureaucratic instrument. seventh, investment-based insurance products. the commission has not introduced a ban on commission and an obligation to provide independent advice, but member states have the possibility to do so. the commission has also adopted rules similar to those in the markets in financial instruments directive. then we have the transitional periods, implementation in 24 months. there is a new annex which sets out the qualification requirements, knowledge for insurance mediation. and we have taken the extrajudicial dispute settlement approach that parliament has decided. overall, we have succeeded in strengthening consumer protection. we have succeeded in establishing uniform rules on the insurance market for the distribution of insurance products. i would like to thank once again all those who have taken the trouble to negotiate with the council over three years. in the end, on the last day of the latvian presidency, we managed to reach a compromise overall. thank you very much.
member of the commission.– mr president, this directive is very much part of our overall drive to increase transparency and to improve consumer protection. it is going to give citizens more choice; it will make sure that those selling insurance understand the products that they are selling, and that those buying insurance better understand what they are buying. so i am very pleased that we have reached this point today and that i have got the chance to congratulate werner langen and the shadow rapporteurs for all their hard work over many months, indeed over many years, as we have heard, in getting this proposal into shape. the directive builds on national regimes of insurance distribution. it sets out a number of minimum standards for insurance distributors to follow, and it broadens the scope of distributors covered, to include companies that sell insurance as an add-on to their core business, like travel companies or car dealers. it also gives legal certainty to insurance companies that sell their products directly to consumers by clarifying how they can register their distributors and the information that they need to give to customers. as we have heard, there are stronger requirements around training and development, and when a product is packaged with an insurance policy as part of a special offer, it will in future be possible to separate the elements of the package so that you can buy the car or the holiday you want, with or without the extra insurance. we want people to be clearer about what they are paying for when they buy or invest in an insurance product. so the directive requires greater transparency on fee structures and on any financial incentives that the distributors may have. the requirement for non-life insurance to produce a simple and standardised product information document, which was added by parliament, is a further strengthening of consumer protection. the directive also includes stronger requirements for the sale of life insurance products with investment elements. it requires suitability tests to be run to help determine whether a product fits a consumer’s profile, and because products covered by mifid ii and the idd are often interchangeable, these rules have, as far as possible, been aligned. there is one small technical point i need to mention for the record. the view of our legal service is that recital 69 of the text is not fully in line with the common understanding on delegated acts. that said, in the context of a general compromise, the commission can accept this wording because generally it does adhere to the common understanding, in accordance with which the commission will, of course, continue to act. this directive ensures a level playing field between different insurance sellers and a more consistent level of consumer protection, in particular by increasing transparency. for me, transparency is essential if we are to legislate in a manner that is proportionate and that avoids unnecessary burdens. by making the right information available, we can help consumers make the right decisions and also encourage responsible behaviour in the sector. the insurance distribution directive is, i believe, an important step in that direction, and that is why i am very pleased today to have the chance to support it. commission’s written statement the wording of the second sentence of recital 69 of the text is not fully in line with the common understanding on delegated acts because it refers to the need for appropriate contacts with parliament and council ahead of the adoption of the delegated act. in the context of a general compromise, the commission can nevertheless accept this wording because it generally adheres to the common understanding that we remain committed to upholding. the commission considers transparency in preparation of delegated acts of paramount importance. the commission will continue to act in accordance with the common understanding and particularly declaration 39 in the area of financial services.

in writing. ‒ a number of the developments in the schengen acquis listed in the report do not in fact constitute 'developments' in the sense of efficient police and judicial cooperation between eu member states. there is therefore no reason to abolish the rules originally codified in the schengen agreement, especially since the current development of the eu also implies that the level of european integration already achieved cannot be maintained permanently.
in writing. ‒ acts from the schengen acquis in the area of police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters which are no longer useful or are not fully implemented in any case can be repealed in good conscience. that is why i voted for this resolution. these acts are now repealed: decision sch/com-ex (93) 14 (combating illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs), decision sch/com ex (97) 13 rev. 2 (abduction of minors), decision sch/com-ex (98) 52 (guidelines on crossborder police cooperation), decision sch/com-ex (99) 11, rev. 2 (violations of traffic rules) and decision 2008/173/jha (sis ii checks).
in writing. ‒ i voted today in favour of the report on the repeal of certain acts in the field of police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters, as i believe that the schengen convention must be developed and updated, especially at this time.
in writing. ‒ some of the schengen acquis acts in the area of police and judicial cooperation are outdated or no longer up to date. either its content has been taken up again in other acts or it is limited in time. the commission's proposal to repeal these acts is therefore correct. it improves the clarity of existing rules.

in writing. ‒ legislation in the field of police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters which is no longer useful must be repealed. that is why i voted for this resolution. the following acts are hereby repealed: joint action 96/610/jha (register of skills and expertise in the field of counter-terrorism), joint action 96/699/jha (compilation of chemical profiles of drugs), joint action 96/747/jha (register of skills and expertise in the field of organised crime), joint action 96/750/jha (combating drug addiction and trafficking), joint action 97/339/jha (cooperation in the field of public policy and security), joint action 97/372/jha (cooperation between customs authorities), joint action 98/c 216/01 and the council convention of 17 june 1998 (driving licences), joint action 98/427/jha (application of best practices in legal assistance in criminal matters) in the framework of the european regulation (jha) no 2008/978. these specific joint actions have not been abolished per se but have already been incorporated into other legal texts. but why does the eu have to regulate the withdrawal of driving licences for all member states?
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the recommendation for a decision to join the enlarged commission of the convention for the conservation of southern bluefin tuna, as i consider the conservation of this species in our waters to be an important contribution of europe to biodiversity. per capita consumption of fish is increasing by one to two percent each year. in addition, the number of people is growing by well over one percent a year. so humanity is demanding two to three percent more fish on the table every year. all species of bluefin tuna are on the iucn red list. the southern species is classified as 'endangered', the atlantic and mediterranean species as 'highly endangered', and the pacific bluefin tuna has been classified as 'vulnerable' since last november. this has to be stopped.
in writing. ‒ this decision is a coherent continuation of the objectives of a sustainable policy. the protection of highly migratory species is a particular challenge. this is why it is important that countries have a strong exchange of ideas. the problem of illegal fishing must continue to be addressed. the enlarged commission will give europe greater responsibility in this area.
in writing. ‒ the southern bluefin tuna (thunnus maccoyii) resolution is not about the reciprocal exchange of best-practice recipes for sushi and sashimi, but about another regulation of the eu's external fisheries relations to protect the most overfished tuna species in the world. since this problem cannot understandably be solved by a single member state alone, a common eu position makes sense. that is why i voted for it. the eu commission is already involved in six regional tuna fisheries organisations. the eu is now becoming a full member of the 'expanded commission of the convention for the conservation of southern bluefin tuna (ccsbt) '. this resolution gives the green light to that. the signature of this international instrument will enable the eu to become a full member of the enlarged ccsbt commission, of which it has been a non-cooperating member since 2006. however, it remains to be seen how and whether the eu can assert its legitimate demands against the permanent overfishing of tuna, especially against japan. and then we will wait and see when the house of lords will table a resolution calling for an eu-wide ban on tuna consumption.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because the new rules on insurance distribution will bring much more clarity, transparency and legal certainty, not only to consumers but also to small insurance agencies, through better information. this also applies to the costs of remunerating insurance intermediaries. the commission also notes that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the compatibility of the aid with the internal market. i support the introduction of the single product sheet, because it will enable consumers to compare the basic information of different insurance products in other member states, as is already the case with other financial products.
in writing. ‒ i voted today in favour of the report on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on insurance mediation (idd) because i support the approach and have given my group a lot of impetus to make it more consumer-friendly. with the idd, the rules on insurance intermediation now apply to all market participants who sell insurance, including for example travel agencies and car rental companies, unless they are 'micro insurance'. in addition, insurance undertakings must provide customers with information on the type of remuneration received by their employees for the distribution of insurance products and, for certain complex life insurance products, also on the total cost of the insurance contract, including consultancy and service costs. it's good for the consumer.
in writing. ‒ with today's report, we are increasing transparency for consumers. at the same time, it ensures that in particular smaller insurance companies will enjoy greater legal certainty in the future. the accessibility of crossborder insurance schemes will also be improved. it allows customers to compare the performance of individual suppliers more easily and quickly.
in writing. ‒ the insurance mediation directive proposal has now been agreed in trilogue with council. it covers sales of general insurance products and takes into account the whole distribution chain. the directive’s approach is geared towards minimum harmonisation, which means that the member states would have enough flexibility to continue with existing practices. this directive includes enhanced information about prices and costs of products, the indication of whether the seller has an incentive or receives a commission for selling a product and the introduction of a standardised product information document for non-life insurance products, aiming to give consumers key elements in a standard format to help them make an informed decision. since many of the problematic elements (such as the requirements for professional development, which were subsequently set at a more proportionate 15 hours a year, and the possibility to unbundle a product from its insurance) were resolved during trilogue, i voted in favour of the report. by the way, in my opinion, the euro must be abolished: it leads to dissension and discord in europe.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the report on reducing inequalities today, with a particular focus on child poverty, because the non-legislative own-initiative report - despite some good approaches - clearly oversteps its target in many areas, disregards the rights of parents and breaches subsidiarity. i am fully in favour of children's rights, but i am equally convinced that this must be done at the appropriate political levels. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment against the adverse effects of certain substances and preparations is therefore a very good one. children need action, not words.
in writing. ‒ child poverty is still a sad reality in europe. we must be firm in our opposition. children are the future of our ageing society. i therefore welcome this report and will continue to work to reduce social inequalities and to ensure that education is accessible to all.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the own-initiative report by mrs zuber on reducing inequalities, with a particular focus on child poverty, because the report - despite some good approaches - clearly oversteps its target in many areas, disregards the rights of parents and breaches subsidiarity. i am fully in favour of children's rights, but i am equally convinced that this must be done at the appropriate political levels. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment against the adverse effects of certain substances and preparations is therefore a very good one. children need action, not words. i am also of the opinion that the euro must be abolished because it is causing discord and division in europe!
in writing. i consider this report to be a very important initiative of parliament. much more attention needs to be paid to the issue of child poverty. children in europe are increasingly at risk of poverty and social exclusion. statistics show that a quarter of all children in the eu experience poverty and social exclusion. in 2013, 26.5 million children were at risk of poverty or social exclusion, and since 2008, two thirds of eu member states have experienced an increase in child poverty. we must counteract this. childhood poverty can have lifelong effects. children who grow up in poverty are at greater risk of being poor as adults. every child should have the opportunity to reach their full potential. but we must also be careful not to go too far in our efforts to identify and tackle the causes of child poverty. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. the promotion of flexible working relationships in my view does not in any way lead to a weakening of the social rights of children (§ 10); i cannot agree to the right to adequate and appropriate housing (article 18); nor can i support a guaranteed right of women to sexual and reproductive health (§ 38).

in writing. ‒ i voted against the non-legislative own-initiative report on cohesion policy and marginalised groups today, because such a document makes no sense when it is published less than a year after all the eu's long-term financial plans have been adopted. the report also misses the point on many points: the eu cannot and must not try to solve everything by taking on more and more power. many problems - particularly in cohesion policy - require adapted regulation at national, regional and local level. that is subsidiarity.
in writing. ‒ cohesion policy is one of the main european instruments for reducing social inequalities in different regions of europe. the problem of social exclusion has increased in the wake of the economic crisis. it is unacceptable that some groups of the population continue to lack adequate access to existing infrastructure and sanitation facilities. i therefore welcome the fact that this report is being used to promote greater social cohesion.
in writing. ‒ the own-initiative report recommends changes in the eu's cohesion policy. this eu policy area accounts for more than one third of the total eu budget and aims to reduce economic and social inequalities in europe and thus strengthen social cohesion. the report calls for greater attention to be paid to supporting marginalised groups in society, in particular roma communities and the needs of women. the commission has also been active in the field of employment policy, and has been involved in the preparation of the white paper on growth and employment. as the report itself points out, the legal basis for cohesion policy already contains a number of provisions to support marginalised groups in society. in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, it is the responsibility of the eu member states to implement these requirements in the context of operational programmes. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of the environment and to improve the quality of life in the member states. i therefore voted against the report. i am also of the opinion that the euro must be abolished because it is causing discord and division in europe!

in writing. ‒ i voted against the draft european resolution on 'cohesion policy and marginalised groups' because i think it is a mockery to want to pursue minority policy while the european peoples are facing the asylum crisis with their backs to the wall. the eu's first concern is the preservation of europe, its cultures and its peoples, not any minorities, many of whom are - as in the case of many so-called 'refugees' - de facto wealth migrants.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament is the 'announcing body'. an entire resolution deals with political guidelines for cohesion policy for the benefit of the most marginalised groups in society. however, the same resolution states at the outset that there is no definition of the term 'social marginalised group'. the first paragraph calls on the european commission to provide guidelines for the definition of the term 'social marginalised groups', which does not yet exist. this is a parliamentary nonsense which wastes taxpayers' money and does not provide practical solutions to problems. that is why i voted against this resolution. if there are indeed problems with hitherto undefined social marginal groups in regions of the member states, then these regions of the member states are also best placed to find and implement appropriate solutions but not the eu.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because, particularly in view of the existing and new security policy challenges (refugee issue, is), we cannot find solutions in the eu alone and in isolation. it requires a common solution of all the states. only together with the united nations will we be able to promote peace, security and progress in the world and in europe. the eu must therefore play a more important role within the general assembly.
in writing. ‒ i am opposed today to the non-legislative own-initiative report on the subject 'the role of the eu within the united nations: how can the eu's foreign policy objectives be better achieved? voted in favour of the resolution, as i believe that the approach taken there is wrong in terms of strengthening the eu's role in the un. i believe that we need more pragmatic action, rather than ideological positions, to achieve more in the world.
in writing. ‒ many european challenges need to be solved internationally. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. this requires a stronger eu positioning within the un. comprehensive reforms are also needed to meet the new challenges of a changing world.
in writing. ‒ the own-initiative report aims to clearly define the role of the european union within the united nations. the eu is also committed to the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, and to the promotion of the rule of law and respect for human rights. the report rightly points out that the security council urgently needs to be reformed in order to maintain its capacity to act effectively, as in its current composition it does not represent a geographically balanced representation of interests but still reflects the geopolitical conditions of 1945. i am in favour of germany's permanent seat on the security council, because today, as the third largest contributor to the united nations, germany has considerably less influence on the united nations and in particular on the security council than the five veto powers. further reforms of the united nations are also needed. however, the report calls for a permanent seat for the eu in the security council, even though the eu is not a state but an international organisation and as such cannot be a member of the united nations under the current rules. that is why i rejected the report. i am also of the opinion that the euro must be abolished because it is causing discord and division in europe!

in writing. - why call the moon? the european parliament acts as the "notification body". that is why i reject this resolution. the eu is already represented at the united nations by a wide range of actors: the president of the european council, the 'eu foreign minister', the european commission. the member states have their permanent representatives, two of whom (france and the united kingdom) are also permanent members of the security council with the right of veto. the treaty already obliges the member states to coordinate their positions and actions in all international fora. the european union has already de facto abolished its own responsibility for foreign policy and the design of its relations with the un system. i reject the idea that the eu should speak and decide in place of the 28 member states, and in the medium term even replace france and the united kingdom on the security council. this is a problem that is both a blank check and a potential source of division between the member states.
i have to say that i am not in favour of this. the commission is not prepared to accept this. equal treatment for all is the central issue, not only in the question of speaking time but also, of course, in the question of tax payments. we find that no, there is no fair tax competition. unfortunately, the revelations that were made by investigative journalists last year in the wake of the luxleaks scandal have revealed that some - and not just a few, but many, especially international - companies are able to exploit tax loopholes. they have aggressive tax avoidance models that result in them reducing their tax burden greatly. the figures on the table are worrying, when disney, for example, can reduce its tax burden to 0.3% on a billion-dollar profit, when, conversely, it is clear to the british house of commons, for example, that facebook paid only £5,000 in corporation tax in 2014, less than the average facebook employee, who earns £26,500 and has to pay £5,393 in income tax, including insurance. it's not fair. the competitive disadvantage for small and medium-sized enterprises is particularly significant. the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has been informed by scientists that smes are at a disadvantage of 20 to 25% compared with large companies. it was therefore necessary for this parliament to set up the special committee, as i proposed here a year ago. we worked hard. we were in luxembourg, belgium, the netherlands, ireland, but also in the uk and outside the eu in switzerland. we have also invited representatives from so-called tax havens. we talked extensively with the ngos and the tax experts from independent institutes, universities, and we wanted to hear from the corporations as well. unfortunately, it took a very long time for the international corporations facebook, google, amazon, hsbc and barclays to even be willing to come into our parliament. we should all agree that such disregard for parliament must not be allowed to recur in the future. we have to be united here. we have drawn up a whole series of proposals on how we can achieve fairer tax competition in the future. the combination of 28 national tax laws creates loopholes which a few - our thoughts of sympathy to the victims, their families, the city of paris and all the other victims of terrorism, and you have spoken of them. today, more than ever, we need solidarity in action against the scourge of terrorism. a decisive action, capable of defending our freedoms, our values, but also the security of our fellow citizens. we need the widest and most intensive european cooperation possible, and it must involve all those who are willing to join us in this relentless struggle against those who sow terror, who kill blindly. never has there been such a need for a strong and decisive europe, capable of taking swift, coordinated and firm action. the presidency, after the paris attacks, immediately convened an extraordinary justice and home affairs council on 20 november, at the end of which ambitious actions were decided upon. the council decided to confirm its commitment to the fight against terrorism by focusing on operational measures. it is essential that we mobilise all our energies to achieve results and make our societies safer. let me now explain the measures adopted. the council also called on the commission to take the necessary steps to ensure that the pnr system is implemented at european level. the presidency hopes to reach an agreement with parliament at the next trilogue and we are fully aware of the importance for you of concluding the negotiations on the data protection package. the presidency reiterates its commitment to also finalize the negotiations before the end of the year. as regards the trafficking of firearms, the council is working to combat illegal arms trafficking more effectively within the european union, drawing on revised texts and operations carried out in the framework of the so-called european union policy cycle to combat large-scale international organised crime. the presidency will begin discussions this week on the proposal for a revision of the firearms directive which the commission has just presented. as regards the reinforcement of external border controls, member states undertake to implement immediately the necessary systematic and coordinated controls at the external borders, including on persons enjoying the right of free movement. the terrorist in the jewish museum in brussels had a european passport, and the terrorists who acted in paris in january, in copenhagen and again in paris on 13 november had, for some of them, european passports. i would ask parliament to take account of this reality and the expectations of our fellow citizens. a modernisation of the border control systems of the schengen member states will be implemented by march 2016. as regards third-country nationals, member states shall systematically register, including fingerprinting, third-country nationals entering the schengen area and carry out systematic security checks using the relevant databases. finally, member states will reinforce controls at the most exposed external borders, including by deploying, where the situation so requires, rapid border intervention teams and police officers to ensure that screening and security checks are carried out in a systematic manner. as regards the exchange of information, the council undertook to implement a series of actions aimed at making the best use of the tools put in place and at allowing the most effective cooperation possible. member states will thus ensure that national authorities systematically enter data on all suspected foreign terrorist fighters into the sis ii database. the council welcomed the establishment of the european centre for the fight against terrorism at europol on 1 january. the new europol regulation, on which we hope to reach agreement without delay, should be consistent with the mandate and objectives of the centre, including the internet content reporting unit. member states will second counter-terrorism experts to the centre to form a reinforced cross-border investigation support unit capable of providing rapid and comprehensive support to investigators in the event of a major terrorist incident in the european union. the council invited the commission to submit a legislative proposal to enable europol to make systematic cross-checks between its databases and those of sis ii. in terms of the fight against terrorist financing, the council invited the commission to submit proposals to strengthen, harmonise and improve the competences of financial intelligence units and their cooperation with each other, and to ensure that these units have rapid access to the information needed to increase the effectiveness and efficiency of the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing. the council also recommended that controls on non-bank payment methods be strengthened. in the context of judicial responses to terrorism and violent extremism, the council notes with satisfaction the signing by the union, in riga on 22 october, in writing. ‒ the resolution notes that the impact of draft amending budget no 8/2015 is a eur 9 403,4 million reduction in member states’ contribution to the union budget. it is, however, highlighted that additional means are needed to address the refugee crisis, both along the transit routes and for their reception in europe’s cities, and that the financial pledges for the agencies supporting refugees are still lagging behind by eur 2,3 billion. even though a firm compromise could not be reached to use the reflow to address the refugee crisis, i have voted in favour of the resolution since the position of the council was approved and the amending budget adopted. by the way, in my opinion the euro must be abolished. it leads to dissension and discord in europe.
in writing. ‒ providing additional financial resources to address the challenges of hosting an unprecedented number of refugees in european cities and regions cannot be in the spirit of responsible policy towards the peoples of europe. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the situation in the former yugoslavia is not further complicated by the fact that the situation in the former yugoslavia is not yet fully resolved.
in writing. ‒ i have agreed to the european parliament resolution on amending budget no 8/2015 on own resources and the european data protection supervisor. this is a standard exercise, in particular to adapt the annual contributions of the member states to the circumstances. the sum is to be charged to the member states.
in writing. ‒ i abstained today from voting on the report on the mobilisation of the flexibility instrument for urgent budgetary measures under the european agenda on migration, as i support the concern the eu's ability to act in this crisis situation . at the same time, i regard the use of the accelerated procedure without sufficient consultation of parliament and its committees as a very bad idea.
in writing. ‒ i support the use of the flexibility instrument. we need sufficient financial support to meet the challenges of the ongoing refugee crisis. the importance of the eu having sufficient flexibility in its budgeting is becoming clearer.
in writing. ‒ the proposal to mobilise the flexibility instrument was published together with commission letter of amendment 2/2016 of 14 october 2015. this mobilisation concerns an amount of eur 1.5 billion over the ceiling of the multiannual financial framework (mff) in heading 3 and eur 24 million in heading 4 and is intended to finance support measures for the management of the refugee crisis. in principle, i am in favour of the adoption of measures to deal with the migration and refugee crisis and of the use of the flexibility instrument in exceptional circumstances. however, i believe there is more scope for a reshuffle in the 2016 budget. there are a number of budget lines with poor implementation and no demonstrable eu added value that could be cut to help tackle the migration and refugee crisis. this requires a comprehensive eu approach, as we in alfa have already suggested weeks ago. this includes measures such as comprehensive control of the eu's external borders, the establishment of transit zones outside the schengen area and the consistent return of rejected asylum seekers. i have abstained on this point because it is still pending.
in writing. ‒ the proposal to mobilise the flexibility instrument was published together with commission letter of amendment 2/2016 of 14 october 2015. this mobilisation concerns an amount of eur 1.5 billion over the ceiling of the multiannual financial framework (mff) in heading 3 and eur 24 million in heading 4 and is intended to finance support measures for the management of the refugee crisis. the european union is committed to the development of a common foreign and security policy. i therefore support the use of the flexibility instrument in these exceptional circumstances. it is important and right that the eu also makes a fairly large financial contribution. that's why i agreed to the proposal.

in writing. ‒ i voted today in favour of the report on the mobilisation of the european union solidarity fund to provide advances in the 2016 budget. eu assistance to member states and candidate countries affected by floods or other natural disasters is handled through the european union solidarity fund (eusf). this makes the eusf one of the most visible and effective examples of eu solidarity.
in writing. ‒ the european solidarity fund supports countries that have been severely affected by natural disasters. at the same time, this fund is also an important sign of european solidarity towards other countries. i therefore vote in favour of the provision of sufficient financial resources in the budget of the european union for the coming year.
in writing. ‒ the proposal regarding the european union solidarity fund (eusf) aims at including in the 2016 general budget of the european union eur 50 million for the timely and efficient payment of advances should a natural disaster strike a european region in the coming year. the eusf is used to respond to situations caused by natural disasters; both in member states and in countries involved in accession negotiations, and thus sends a message of solidarity while assisting citizens. this is why i have voted in favour of this resolution. by the way, in my opinion the euro must be abolished. it leads to dissension and discord in europe.

in writing. ‒ the agreement between the council, the commission and parliament on the 2016 budget amounts to eur 155 billion in commitment appropriations and eur 143.8 billion in payment appropriations. this represents an unjustified increase of 6,7% in commitments and 1,8% in payments compared to 2015. the commission has also adopted a communication on the implementation of the european year of the environment, which aims to promote the use of renewable energy sources in the european union. but almost all the margins were used up instead of re-establishing budgetary priorities. the council itself argued that parliament should narrow its priorities as the increases proposed by parliament collectively exhausted the margins in the areas of growth and employment (headline 1a), cohesion (headline 1b) and security and citizenship (headline 3). this puts at risk the functioning of the 2014-2020 multiannual financial framework (mff). the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the budgetary authority is able to meet its obligations. i cannot agree to an ever-increasing eu budget without real priorities. that is why i voted against the report. i am also of the opinion that the euro must be abolished because it is causing discord and division in europe!

in writing. ‒ i voted against the european parliament resolution on the 2016 budgetary procedure and the general budget. the eu budget is bloated, financing a multitude of tasks that cannot be decided at eu level and therefore violates the principle of subsidiarity as well as national responsibility. the budget is based on the principle of perpetual motion: the eu was born out of the common agricultural policy, but today has grown out of it. however, a large part of the budget is used to subsidize the agricultural sector. the budget therefore reflects the fact that the eu has become more and more, but rarely wiser. it is time for fundamental and unabashed reform. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. until then, all i can say is no.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the rejection report under rule 106 of the rules of procedure: authorisation of uses of diethylhexylphthalate (dehp) for purely technical and political reasons, as the eu commission is using the instrument of implementing powers, although the area is not covered by the agreements with parliament. i cannot agree to such an overstepping of authority.
in writing. ‒ dehp is a chemical used in the production of plastics. as an important component, it makes the plastic to be produced more elastic. however, dehp can also present a significant potential for harm to human health and the environment. that is why i support this motion.
in writing. ‒ this objection rejects the authorisation of the use of diethylhexylphthalate (dehp) in recycled pvc. this objection rejects the authorisation decision of the european chemicals agency (echa) on the grounds that it is incompatible with the reach regulation. reach is the european regulation on the registration, evaluation, authorisation and restriction of chemical substances. echa concluded that there is a minimal risk to consumers. the objection ignores the far-reaching impact on the circular economy, which is intended to promote recycling in europe, and the increased environmental damage caused by the production of newly produced pvc without any recycling. i voted against the objection because i consider scientific advice to be important and do not want political disputes to determine legislation. parliament should support the circular economy and promote transparency with regard to the reach regulation. i am also of the opinion that the single euro must be abolished, because it is leading to discord and division in europe.
in writing. ‒ i did not vote for the european parliament resolution on the refusal to authorise uses of diethylhexylphthalate (dehp) under article 106 of the ec treaty. it's about the scientific question of whether or not you can use dehp. the debate revolves around the question of whether there is a scientifically certain threshold of harmfulness. i have followed the line of my group in this decision.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because we need a full accounting of all the 'obvious' corporate tax practices of the member states concerned. i also think that this includes the mandatory ad hoc exchange of information on national tax rulings, so that fair tax competition can be ensured in the future. deals end up with tax evasion and a tax increase for all other taxpayers. we therefore have an obligation as members of the european parliament, as representatives of our citizens, to do our part in the fight against illegal practices of tax avoidance and evasion.
in writing. ‒ gue/ngl welcomes the substance of the report by the special committee on tax rulings and other measures similar in nature or effect (taxe). it contains useful proposals for greater tax justice and reflects the negative impact of austerity on tax fairness. despite our many contributions to the report’s final shape, we abstained in today’s vote for the following reasons: political responsibility for tax dumping in the eu has not been fully established and the report does not call for the necessary prolongation of the current mandate; access to documents by the council, the commission and member states remained unsatisfactory; multinational corporations only responded after repeated invitations to taxe, no legal base for sanctions could be established yet and they could not be interrogated thoroughly. moreover, contradictions by the commission president, jean-claude juncker, during his testimony to taxe were not followed up. substance-wise, core issues lack ambition beyond what the commission has proposed already. tax rulings should be made public and tax secrecy laws adjusted. we welcome the idea of consolidating the tax base. however, we miss a clear commitment to broadening the tax base and we criticise the interim period before consolidation which allows for cross-border loss/profit offsetting and no further backstops to prevent tax competition between eu countries.
in writing. ‒ together with my colleagues from the epp group, i am campaigning for companies to pay their taxes in the countries where they actually carry out their economic activity. it is important that we have a better exchange of tax data in the future. this is the only way to develop uniform standards. unless member states work more closely together on this, there will continue to be potential tax loopholes for resourceful companies. once again, it is clear that acting together in europe makes us stronger.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament responded to the luxleaks revelations by setting up a special committee on the role and impact of tax rulings. i supported the establishment of this special committee and voted for the report. alfa is committed to ensuring that all companies and citizens are taxed according to their ability to pay and actually pay these taxes. we need a functioning european regulatory framework in tax law. i am also of the opinion that the euro must be abolished because it is causing discord and division in europe!
in writing. ‒ the european parliament has responded to the luxleaks revelations by setting up a special committee on the role and impact of tax rulings. i support this report: alfa is committed to ensuring that all companies and citizens are taxed according to their ability to pay and actually pay these taxes. we need a functioning european regulatory framework in tax law. the report calls for measures such as a common corporate tax base and automatic exchange of information on tax rulings. these measures are designed to make competition between member states more transparent and to clarify the rules of the game. the measures will help to make discrimination in the field of international tax law more difficult. they restore fair conditions of competition both between member states and between undertakings. the tax competition between member states is preserved. it helps to tame government spending behaviour, binds it to taxpayers' wishes and encourages innovation. the right of the states to decide on the level of tax rates in a completely autonomous manner is not restricted. but tax justice would be greatly improved by the measures, for the benefit of citizens and smes.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament responded to the luxleaks revelations by setting up a special committee on the role and impact of tax rulings. i supported the establishment of this special committee and voted for the report. alfa is committed to ensuring that all companies and citizens are taxed according to their ability to pay and actually pay these taxes. we need a functioning european regulatory framework in tax law. the report calls for measures such as a common corporate tax base and automatic exchange of information on tax rulings. these measures are designed to make competition between member states more transparent and to clarify the rules of the game. the measures will help to make discrimination in and through international tax law more difficult. they restore fair conditions of competition, both between member states and between firms. the tax competition between member states is preserved. it helps to tame government spending behaviour, binds it to taxpayers' wishes and encourages innovation. the right of the states to decide on the level of tax rates in a completely autonomous manner is not restricted. but tax fairness would be significantly improved by the measures for the benefit of citizens and smes.
in writing. ‒ was the work of the taxe special committee worthwhile? i have attended all hearings - from trade union representatives, business associations, the big four audit firms to journalists who have played a significant role in the publication of controversial tax practices. we have shed some light on the tax avoidance policies of companies and member states. the cost to honest taxpayers and small and medium-sized enterprises is at least eur 70 billion. so our demands are justified: we must create a framework for fair tax competition and close loopholes for multinational companies. qualified specialists in tax administrations must be recruited to ensure that they fulfil their control obligations. we need clear transparency rules to deal with conflicts of interest. finally, agreement seems to be on the principle that companies tax their profits where they are generated. a responsible tax strategy must be part of every corporate social responsibility reporting. the epp welcomes the exemption for smes in the disclosure of accounts, which will be made country-specific. i agree with the proposal that our mandate as a special committee be extended because a number of documents have been withheld from us so far. the interim report adopted today can only be a first step towards more tax justice in the eu.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament responded to the luxleaks revelations by setting up a special committee on the role and impact of tax rulings. alfa is committed to ensuring that all companies and citizens are taxed according to their ability to pay and actually pay these taxes. we need a functioning european regulatory framework in tax law. the report calls for measures such as a common corporate tax base and automatic exchange of information on tax rulings. the tax competition between member states has thus far been maintained. it is a central liberal element in my view. competition helps to tame government spending behaviour, binds it to taxpayers' wishes and stimulates innovation. although tax competition has so far been maintained through tax rates, i fear that the commission may abuse this first step towards tax harmonization in the future. if it were to harmonise the tax rates according to the tax base, then tax competition would be abolished. that is why i voted against this report.

in writing. ‒ the report identifies a number of actions that should be taken at european level to combat terrorism. the recent terrorist attacks in paris in particular have shown the urgency of such measures. the report focuses in particular on the prevention of radicalisation and recruitment of eu citizens by terrorist organisations and calls for an action plan by the commission to this end. the rapporteur highlights, among other things, the problem of radicalisation often taking place in overcrowded prisons, which is why guidelines and training for staff and educational programmes for prisoners to prevent radicalisation in prisons should be implemented. other areas of action include tackling online recruitment, training in educational institutions, the need for an eu directive on passenger name record (pnr) data, and enhanced cooperation between law enforcement agencies in the member states within existing systems. this includes, for example, the schengen information system (sis) and other platforms. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. i am also of the opinion that the euro must be abolished because it is causing discord and division in europe!

president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank you for inviting the council presidency to take part in this debate on cooperation with turkey and in particular on the results of the summit held on sunday. the presidency welcomes the outcome of this summit, which was organized on the initiative of the president of the european council and which you attended throughout, mr president. the first vice-president of the commission, mr timmermans, who negotiated the action plan with the turkish authorities, should also be thanked and congratulated for his commitment. this summit meeting was very timely, because it was able to address issues of vital importance to the security of the union. our relations with turkey, particularly in the present context, are of considerable importance, both on migration issues and in the wider context of our relations. we share many common interests with turkey and our cooperation is indispensable in the face of the three major crises affecting us and turkey. firstly, the war in syria and the absolute need to find a political solution to this particularly deadly and destabilising conflict. the second is the refugee problem, which is directly linked to this conflict, and finally terrorism, which has hit paris, but has also hit turkey and elsewhere and which must be fought relentlessly. the summit has produced concrete results and confirmed the need for increased cooperation and regular dialogue. the revitalization of our relations, the liberalization of the visa regime, the rules on readmission, and humanitarian and financial aid for the 2 million refugees in syria are precisely concrete results. it must also be said that everything we have agreed with turkey must nevertheless encourage us to continue what we are doing within the european union. all the measures concerning better surveillance of our borders, better control of our external borders, relocation policies, the various other border measures must of course be continued, so we must implement everything that has been decided and everything that has yet to be decided must be done quickly. you will understand, mr president, that it is not the presidency's place to present the summit's outcome in detail. it would be more appropriate if the vice-president, the first vice-president of the commission, were to give you his assessment of this meeting. however, as the summit's final declaration noted, all the elements agreed on sunday will have to be developed in parallel and carefully evaluated. and this also applies to the accession process, whereby all the conditions applicable to all the applicant countries are of course also applicable to turkey. the council will pay particular attention to ensuring that the measures adopted last sunday are implemented in full and in a spirit of solidarity. and of course parliament will be fully informed of the follow-up to these decisions.
first vice-president of the commission.– mr president, president jean-claude juncker has asked me to debrief you on his behalf since i was also at the summit. by the way, president schulz, you yourself were at the summit. you intervened and you were there for the whole duration of the summit, so parliament was very well represented and was an integral part of our decision-making. i hope president schulz will share jean-claude juncker’s view and my view that this summit was fruitful and opened a new chapter in the eu’s partnership with turkey. since april, the eu has held four meetings at heads of state and government level to discuss the migration crisis. at each of these meetings we said it was necessary to engage with turkey – and this is what we did on sunday. it is clear that we need to cooperate to secure our borders, jointly to bring order into migratory flows, and to stem irregular migration. but the focus of the summit went far beyond the current refugee crisis. turkey is a strategic partner for europe in many areas: trade, the economy, foreign policy, energy and customs. at the summit, we reached agreement on how to move forward in all key areas of our cooperation. we agreed on the need for a structured, frequent and more dynamic high-level dialogue. we decided to have summits twice a year to discuss mutual relations and international issues. we hope that the meeting created a new partnership both on refugee-related matters and beyond. to name one example, the recent and atrocious attacks in paris and ankara – including a bomb again last night – showed how europe and turkey are confronted by the same security threats, and they reinforced our resolve to step up counter-terrorism cooperation, which should be a strong focus of this dialogue. this new chapter of our relationship, and now our partnership, will not lead to a situation in which we forget the remaining divergences and differences we may have with turkey – on human rights and freedom of the press. all of these will be matters to which we will come back again and again. we need to work with turkey in order to narrow the gap between our positions. the proof of the pudding is in the eating. the commission is now working to ensure that implementation is swift, effective and immediate. the commission will prepare a report on the state of play for the 15 december european council. to go more specifically into what was agreed: firstly, re-energising the eu-turkey relationship must also mean putting new energy into the ongoing accession negotiations. the summit declaration jointly welcomes the decision to hold the intergovernmental conference on 14 december for the opening of chapter 17 on economic and monetary union. in a letter sent by president juncker to prime minister davutoğlu, the commission reiterated its commitment to complete the preparatory work for the opening, in the first quarter of 2016, of chapters 15, on energy; 23, on judiciary and fundamental rights; 24, on justice, freedom and security; 26, on education and culture; and 31, on foreign, security and defence policy. secondly, turkey has committed to accelerating the fulfilment of the visa liberalisation benchmarks, and we welcome that. the commission will assist turkey in this endeavour, and strive to achieve visa liberalisation for turkish citizens in the schengen area by october 2016, provided, of course, that all requirements have been met by then. we want to accelerate the process but we do not want to change the requirements. they will remain firm and they need to be applied in full. by the way, turkey did not ask us to relax the requirements. progress needs to be made on the management of borders, asylum and migration, quality of travel documents and respect for minorities’ rights. moreover, the visa liberalisation process can only go hand in hand with substantial progress on the eu-turkey readmission agreement, notably on the obligation to take back third-country nationals. the date for full implementation of the readmission agreement has been considerably brought forward, to june 2016, from the initially proposed date of october 2017. thirdly, we agreed on addressing the refugee crisis together. we agreed to activate the joint action plan that was agreed ad referenda on 15 october and welcomed by heads of state and government of the eu’s 28 member states at the european council held the same day. this is a joint action plan to step up cooperation on migration management in a coordinated effort to tackle the refugee crisis. it identifies a series of actions for both the european union and the republic of turkey. the aim is twofold: this is about confronting common challenges in a concerted manner and supplementing turkey’s efforts in managing the large number of people in need of international protection in the country. on sunday, turkey committed to implementing immediately the elements agreed on in the action plan, notably immediate action to stem the flow of irregular migrants to the eu and to improve the socio-economic situation of syrians under temporary protection in turkey. both sides reaffirmed their shared commitment to step up the fight against smugglers. the eu has committed to providing immediate and ongoing humanitarian assistance in turkey, including through its overall financial support. the commission has put forward its decision: the turkey refugee facility was adopted last week. on sunday there was consensus among leaders that the eu is committed to providing an initial eur 3 billion of additional resources. the need for, and nature of, this funding will be reviewed in the light of the developing situation. the details will be worked out with the eu member states by the next european council. however, let me be crystal clear about the destination for these funds: this is not money for turkey – it is money to provide help to refugees in turkey. this is money to provide for medical care for syrians, for schooling, and for better living conditions for syrian refugees in turkey. i hope this house will not question the importance of burden-sharing, not only within the eu but also with all our neighbours. we have put in place several instruments for that: the syrian trust fund, the african trust fund and the turkey refugee facility. let me finish on the question of resettlement. i have repeatedly stressed, including before you, that you take a lot of human misery out of the equation if you have resettlement. you take the criminal networks out of the equation – with all the risks that people take to come to europe – and you introduce fair burden sharing by the international community. and, by the way, you can identify precisely who you invite to come to europe. resettlement is part of the overall partnership with turkey set out on sunday. it is explicitly referred to under point 6 of the summit declaration. the next steps on resettlement were discussed on the margins of the summit. the commission will prepare a framework for such a voluntary scheme by 15 december. i want to repeat what president juncker has said: this will be an open and voluntary process. those member states willing to join this common undertaking will tell us – yes or no – whether they would like to be part of this endeavour, which the commission deems very necessary.
